A BLACK MASK ROMANCE.
SECRET HISTORY OF BALD-KNOB-BERISM IN MISSOURI.
Actual Strength of the Order-How Bill Walker's Sweetheart's Brother Betrayed Him to the Law-The Intended Lynching of Col. Harrington.

Ozark (Me.) correspondence of the Globe-Democrat Col. Almus Harrington, of Ozark, associate counsel for the State in the Bald Knobber cases on the 24th instant, gave the Globe-Democrat correspondent some of the unwritten history of the black mask order in Christian county, and talked freely of the methods employed by the prosecution in the identification of the Edens-Green murderers and the secret work used in the capture of Bill Walker.

"I have been too busy up to this time to talk to newspaper men about the Bald Knobbers," said the attorney as the Globe-Democrat's correspondent made known his interviewing inclinations, "and before the conviction of Chief Walker and the principal actors in the Edens-Green tragedy, it would not have been policy for the prosecution to make any statement to the public about the case. Now, since the Knobbers have been tried and convicted, I will give you some facts that up to this time have only been known inside the organization and by the prosecution and a few of the State's secret allies. Among all the stories of criminal adventures I ever read there was not as much material for genuine romance as in the bare fact of this Bald Knobber movement. In this case, at least, 'Truth is stranger than fiction.' I know the whole history of the organization, from its inception in Taney county, in 1885, down to the conviction of the Knobber chief, Dave Walker, last week.

THE FIRST KNOBERS IN CHRISTIAN COUNTY.

"You want to know when and where the first Bald Knob organization was formed in Christian county? Well, the first company was organized in April, 1886, on Bull creek. Among the members of that company who have since become prominent in the history of the organization were Dave Walker, Wm. Walker, Wiley Matthews, Sherman Walker and Wm. Stanley. That company contained at first only eleven members. From that time till the following June was the most active period of organization in Christian county. Judge R. L. Hale joined the order in June, 1886. I know the man who first 'felt' of the judge on the subject of joining the Knobbers. Hale was then in his field plowing, but that is not a matter of much interest. As I said, most of the Bald Knob organizations in Christian county
tide of Bald Knobbism in Christian county was about the time of the first whisky raid. The movement had not then developed its more savage tendencies, and the pouring out of the whisky gave a coloring of justification to the order. But one or two men were whipped before the first Chadwick whisky raid, and the people generally had not realized the approaching crisis.

"I had fought the organization from its birth, and when the Edens-Green murder occurred I determined not to take a fee in defense of one of the men engaged in that crime. When Bud Roy was arrested on the affidavit of Mrs. Green, the Sunday after the murder, he sent a friend to see me. I had been Roy's attorney in a number of cases and was on very intimate terms with him. He sent word to me that he was innocent of the murder, but had attended the meeting at the smelter the night of the killing. I went at once to see Roy and told him his only salvation was to tell all he knew about the meeting before the raid on the Edens and Greens. Roy then gave the sheriff a full list of the names of the men who attended the smelter meeting, and on this information Walker and his band were arrested. When Walker and every man in the Edens-Green raid were arrested and brought to Ozark the Knobbers knew that somebody had given the secret away, and Joe Inman soon broke down and told the first story of the murder. Charley Graves followed Inman and made a confession, but this was kept a close secret by the prosecution.

THE CAPTURE OF BILL WALKER.

"As soon as it was positively known that Bill Walker had been shot in the assault on the Edens-Green family, and that the wounded young Knobber had been taken to Douglas county that night by his father, the capture of the vice-chief seemed to be vitally necessary to complete the chain of evidence against the murderers. Young Walker was also regarded as one of the leading participants in the crime. While down on Bull creek assisting the sheriff in making the arrests, I learned of the relation between Bill Walker and Miss Louisa Newton, Bill Newton's sister. I saw this intimacy between the Walkers and Newton family might be turned to an advantage in the capture of the fugitive vice-chief of the Knobbers. Joe Newton came to Ozark in a few days to see his brother, who was then confined in the court-house with Dave Walkers and other Knobbers arrested for the murder. I told Joe Newton that if he ever expected his brother to receive any mercy from the State he must assist in finding and capturing Bill Walker. Joe Newton was also a Bald Knobber and had the full confidence of Dave Walker. Newton at once agreed, under a promise from the prosecution that his brother would be benefited by the capture of young Walker, to undertake the secret work which he afterwards performed so well. A Negro Dosperado Shot.
(By telegraph to the Dispatch.)
Sr. Louis, August 10.—A special to the Post-Dispatch from Springfield, Mo., says: Bearden, the negro who shot and fatally wounded Officer Palmer Wednesday, was captured to-day, but not until his body had been filled with lead. He was placed in the Springfield jail, which is now surrounded by a mob of 300 men who threaten to lynch the desperado. The negro is so badly wounded, however, that it is thought he will die.

News Summary.
In Wilkesbarre, yesterday, the police made an examination of the bomb found under Williams & Brother's building on Thursday. The bomb was taken into an open field and it exploded with terrific force. It was powerful enough to blow up several blocks of buildings. It is believed that the bomb was placed under the building by an enemy of the Williams Brothers.

Reardon, a colored man, who shot and fatally wounded Policeman Palmer, at Springfield, Missouri, on Thursday, was captured yesterday after having been wounded by his captors, it is thought, fatally. At last accounts the jail was surreounded by a mob of several hundred men, who threatened to lynch Reardon.

The steamer Georgia, of the Norfolk line, struck the mast of the sunken schooner James Phelps yesterday, near Point Lookout, and sustained $800 damage. The spars of the schooner are still standing, and render the channel dangerous to passing vessels.

Burglars entered the residence of F. L. Smith, at Willoughby, near Centreville, Maryland, on Tuesday night, chloroformed Mr. and Mrs Smith, and secured $100 in money. $1000 worth of negotiable paper and a valuable watch.

Hugh M. Brooks, alias W. H. L. Maxwell, convicted of the murder of C. A. Preller, was hanged yesterday in St. Louis. He was executed at the same time and on the same scaffold with Henry Landgraf, the murderer of his sweetheart.

Charles Carroll, of Baltimore, aged 23 years, a descendant of the signer of the Declaration of Independence whose name he bore, was drowned while bathing yesterday at New London, Connecticut.

Amos Miller, colored, charged with having feloniously assaulted a white woman, was taken from the court-room at Franklin, Tennessee, yesterday, by fifty armed men, and lynched.

Lewis Phinney and William Sanford, while track laying on the Fitchburg Railroad, at Concore, Massachusetts, yesterday, were struck and killed by an express train.

The crop report of the Agricultural Department for August shows that corn has advanced from 93 last month to 95 5. Spring wheat has fallen from 95 9 to 87 6.

Frost was reported in Northern Minnesota on Thursday night.

SPRINGFIELD, Mo., Aug. 10.—Si Burden, the negro who fatally shot Policeman Palmer while resisting arrest Wednesday night, was captured at the house of Sandy Eslinger, colored, eight miles east of the city at 5 o'clock this morning by Marshall Barrett and Officers Snow, Hayes and Dameron. When called upon to surrender Burden attempted to draw his pistol to shoot Hayes, wherenpon Snow fired at him twice one shot taking effect in his right breast. BROOKS MEETS DEATH ON THE GALLOWS.
He Leaves a Statement Claiming Innocence and His Blessing for the Authorities.

St. Louis, Aug. 10.—This morning dawned clear and cool and as the first light of Maxwell's last day on earth entered his narrow cell it lengthened the sickly pallor of his face, which had increased during the night. At a few minutes before 5 o'clock Maxwell performed his morning ablution and donned his funeral clothes, which were new, the outer garments being of plain black with a natty fitting Prince Albert coat. At 5:18 Father Tihan arrived and entered the cell, the door of which was closed and those within the jail moved away to give all the privacy possible. Father Tihan then administered communion to the condemned.

At the conclusion of the religious services in Maxwell's cell like offices were accorded Henry Landgraf by Father Tihan. Landgraf had occupied his cot the greater portion of the night after 11:30, and appeared cool and collected. At 5:30 Maxwell and Landgraf sat down to

THEIR FINAL MEAL,

which had been prepared by the jailor's wife. Landgraf ate heartily, while Maxwell partook sparingly. As he sat at the table it was plain to see that all his assumed indifference had departed, and his face was blanched, while a troubled, haunted look had taken possession of his eyes. He was evidently growing weaker, and had lost all hope for staying the executioner's hand. Landgraf maintained the same stolid look. At 6:05 Sheriff Harrington announced that the execution had been postponed two hours. The only reason assigned was that the postponment had been delayed at the request of Maxwell's attorneys. The sheriff stated that the men would leave their cells at 9 o'clock.

MAXWELL'S ADDRESS.
At an early hour this morning Maxwell gave to the press an address of which the following is a part:

"To the People of England: My English countrymen will doubtless remember the great boats that have now and at all times been made by the American people in regard to the fair and just way in which they treat all people. Satisfied that you are not acquainted with the unlawful, unjust and unfair way in which I have been treated, since you are accustomed in England to see justice administered impartially in the courts. The examination of the records in my case will show that the prosecution resorted to every unfair means in their power even to crime itself."

He then went on to detail several instances in which he alleged fraud had been practiced by the prosecution and declared that if he should die he would suffer the penalty of the law without having had a fair trial.

When Martin left the cell of his condemned client, after having notified him that all hope was gone, Maxwell desired to personally thank Fauntleroy for him and handed a letter to Martin for Geresche, in which he thanked Geresche for the efforts made to secure his pardon. Maxwell received the news of his two hours' postponement calmly, though an expression of great relief was plainly visible on his features. Landgraf paid no attention to it in any way. The crowds on the housetops surrounding the jail yard, where the execution took place, remained patiently in their elevated positions, from 5 this morning until the hour of the execution. The number of spectators admitted to the jail was unusually small. For the first time in the history of the St. Louis Four Courts telegraph instruments were placed in the building by the Associated Press and leading papers of the city, for the prompt transmission of news to the public.

The crime for which Landgraff suffered the death penalty was committed on the night of March 5, 1885. The victim was his sweetheart, Annie Tische, a beautiful girl less than 18 years old, whom he murdered because of his jealousy.

STILL HOPING.

At 8:10 o'clock Martin received the following telegram from Fauntleroy, dated at Jefferson City, Mo., which was delivered to Maxwell:

The governor has received another telegram from Minister West, but he persists in the same imposition. Hold as long as possible, as we may hear in time. My heartfelt sympathy to accused and his loved ones Wire my father.

The receipt of this telegram created quite a sensation, as it was the general opinion that the governor would grant, at least, a brief stay. At 8:47 o'clock Sheriff Harrington, proceeded by a detail of police, entered the inner yard of the jail, and the sheriff entered the cell of Maxwell, where both condemned were, and read the death warrants. Maxwell, paled and pulled his fingers nervously, but Landgraf received it stolidly. The men were then bound and the procession to the scaffold was started. As Maxwell passed through the inner yard he walked firmly, but slowly. His face looked pinched and drawn, of ashen hue, and his eyes were swollen. Landgraf looked and moved like a log, with a half smile and half sneer upon his face. The condemned mounted the scaffold without assistance. After Father Tibau had read prayers Maxwell was asked if he had anything to say. He replied with an almost inaudible, "No." Landgraf merely shook his head. The black caps were drawn over their heads. There was an awful look of despair on Maxwell's face as the cap was drawn over his head, and his knees showed weakness. The nooses were adjusted quickly, and at 8:56 the drop fell. Landgraf was pronounced dead in eleven and a half minutes. Maxwell's struggles continued for fourteen minutes, when he, too, was pronounced dead by the attending physicians. The bodies after being cut down were removed to the morgue office and photographed, after which a post mortem was commenced. The necks of both men were broken.

To-day Maxwell furnished a document which he called his dying statement. In it he re-asserts his innocence of the willful killing of Preller, and then gives an epitome of the statement of the case as heretofore published.

STOLE OVER $100,000.
Suicide Breed's Embezzlement Much Larger Than Was Supposed.
HARTFORD, CONK., Sept. 11. It was definitely learned yesterday that the embezzlements of Jon Breed, the assistant cashier of the Hartford National Bank, who recently committed suicide, would aggregate $108,500, instead of $22,000 as was first reported. The estate of Daniel Goodwin loses $98,000; $6,500 is due the Dr. Taft estate, and $16,000 was placed in Mr. Breed's hands for investment by a Hartford gentleman whose name is withheld. The large Shultas estate, of which Breed was the custodian, is intact. The examination of the bank was finished yesterday and not a dollar was missing. Breed lost the money in stock speculations, largely through local brokers.

Traim Mobbers Who Got Nothing.
St. Louis, Sept. 11. A special from Prescott, Arizona, says: The west-bound express train was stopped by three men at Parker's Mill last night. They did not get anything. A reward of $1,500 has been offered for their capture, and Wells, Pargo & Co. will increase the amount.

Narrowly Escaped Lynching.
St. Louis, Sept. 11. St. Beardon, the negro desperado who murdered Officer Pallmore, at Springfield, Ma., August 8, was brought to St. Louis last night and lodged in jail for safe keeping. A mob surrounded the Springfield jail the other night, and Beardon had such a narrow escape from lynching that Sheriff Dodson concluded to bring him to St. Louis.

Emperor William at Bremerhaven.
Bremer, Sept. 11. Emperor William arrived at Bremerhaven at 1:30 oclock this morning. He was received by Herr Lohmann, director of the Nord Deutsche Lloyd Co., and conducted to Lloyd Hall, which was brilliantly illuminated. Later the emperor proceeded to the quay and was rowed to the imperial yacht Hobsonham. The streets were througged and there was great enthusiasm.

THOUGHT SHE WAS HOODOOED.
And Nearly Killed the Girl whom She Suspected of Working the Charm. WICHITA, KAN., Dec. 19 — A remarkble story
And Nearly Killed the Girl whom She Suspected of Working the Charm.

WICHITA, KAN., Dec. 19 — A remarkrble story is told by a merchant from Kingman county.

"Near the little village of Bross, Kingman county," he said, "lives a farmer named Bartlett, with his family, consisting of a son of twenty-one, a daughter of sixteen, and one of eight. The domestic work was done by a negro woman, who was formerly a slave. She imagined that she was hoodooed. The person suspected of having placed the spell on her was the elder daughter of her employer, and she informed the girl of her suspicion. The young lady determined to have some fun out of the old negress, and said she was determined to keep the spell up until her victim was dead. The negress then commenced to design a means of ridding herself of this terrible spell. A few nights ago she and the girl were left alone in the house, while the rest of the family went to a neighbor's. The negress attacked the girl and tied her, hand and foot, stripped her of all her clothing, beat her unmercifully, and concluded her revenge by smearing the girl's body with paint. She then locked her victim up in a room and disappeared. It was not till the following morning that the girl was discovered. She is now in a critical condition. The negress has not yet been found."

THE TORTURED GIRL REPORTED DEAD.

St. Louis, Dec. 19. — Another account says the negress, after painting the girl's body, tied her up in an old fireplace and built a fire about her and then fled. The girl was shortly afterward found by a neighbor and rescued from her perilous position, but she died during the night. The country is being accured for the negress, and if she is found she will be lynched.

BURNED TO BREAK A SPELL. The Wierd and Gruesome Tale of a Kansas Correspondent. ROASTED HER VICTIM ALIVE How a Young Lady On a Farm Was Tortured to Death By a Negro Servant Who Considered Her a Witch. Jennie Barrett's Terrible Fate.
Jennie Barrett's Terrible Fate.

Wichita, Kan., Dec. 19.—Several weeks ago an old negro servant of Eugene Bartlett, a wealthy cattleman of Kingman county, who was known as "good old Rebecca," so George W. Beatty, a well-to-do farmer living near Bross, that county, reported here tonight, conceived the idea that she was being bewitched by Jennie Bartlett, who was about twenty years old. While gradually showing an increased dislike for the lady she kept on with her work, but Saturday, in the presence of the family, she told Jennie that she was being hoodedooed by her and she would have to quit it or there would be trouble. This created considerable merriment, but the old colored woman watched her opp rtunity for breaking the spell.

Last evening early all the family except Jennie went to visit neighbors. Shortly after their departure Robert Donnelly, a young man who lives at Bross, called to see Jennie, as had been his custom for some time, and remained until about 9 o'clock, when Rebecca appeared and stated that there was a very sick horse at the barn, and she wanted him to go up to Bross for some medicine. He left in response to the request.

As soon as the young man was out of hearing, the servant caught the young lady, and tying a rope around her hands, swung her up to a joist with her feet about two feet from the floor. This done she stripped her of her clothes and covered her body with paint and then tar. In a short time she had placed a kettle filled with kindling wood under her, and after putting a large amount of oil on it applied a match.

While the flames were curling around the poor girl's feet and limbs Donnelly returned with the medicine for the sick horse. Before reaching the house he saw a bright light shining through a window and heard frantic screams. He supposed some one had caught fire from an exploded lamp and hastened to the door. The front entrance was locked, and going to a window the horrible spectacle met his eyes. For a moment he scarcely knew what to do, but finally rushed back to the door and broke it open. Then he removed the kettle, cut the rope and conveyed the girl to a resting place. For a few minutes she was unconscious, but she soon recovered sufficiently to tell the story of her flendish treatment. Her feet and lower limbs were burned into a crisp, and a few minutes later death relieved her of the intense agony.

Young Donnelly looked about the house for a few minutes for the assaulting party, and not being able to find her, hastened back to town with the startling news. Over twenty
Young Donnelly looked about the house for a few minutes for the assaulting party, and not being able to find her, hastened back to town with the startling news. Over twenty men were soon on the road to the Bartlethouse to investigate the matter.

A careful investigation failed to find the perpetrator of the crime, but they discovered that one of the horses had disappeared.

A hunt for the negro woman was inaugurated but no word of her capture has been received. The affair has created intense excitement in the neighborhood and every fort possible will be made to effect an arrest.
bross-bross-1888-12.A10: Another lie purporting to give an account of a young woman in Kingman county being burned to death by a negress, was, published in the Kansas City Times yesterday. For heaven's sake stop this idiotic, pointless and malicious circulation of lies about Kansas.—Topeka Journal.
bross-bross-1888-12.A11: The papers last week published a sensational story to the effect that several weeks ago an old negro servant of Eugene Bartlett, a cattleman near Bross, Kingman county, conceived the idea that she was bewitched by Jennie. Bartlett's twenty-year-old daughter, and last night, during the absence of the remainder of the family from home, the negress overpowered the girl, tied her hands and feet, strung her up by her hands to a rafter, striped her of all her clothing, smeared her body with tar and then built a fire in a kettle under her feet and disappeared. When discovered the girl was unconscious, her feet and lower limbs burned to a crisp and other parts of her body also badly burned. She recovered sufficiently to tell how it occurred, but died soon afterward. A searching party has been formed and nothing will be left undone to find the negress.
bross-bross-1888-12.A12: Out in Kansas a colored servant took it into her crazy head that her master's sixteen-year-old daughter was a "hoodoo" and that the hoodooing was especially directed against her. Therefore, when she got the girl alone she stripped her, beat her black and blue, and after painting her body set fire to her. The girl is dead, and the servant is a fugitive from a lynching party that in all probability will succeed in its object. Although no sane person believes in this "hoodoo" rot, yet was the young girl the colored woman's hoodoo. She was the cause—an innocent one, of course—of the servant's crime, and whether captured or not she will suffer all the pangs of being "hoodooed."
bross-bross-1888-12.A15:
She Believed in the Hoodoo.
About three miles from Becoss, a village near Wishita, Kansas, lives Farmer Bartlett, his son and two daughters who came from England a few years ago. They kept a negro woman, who had been a slave, as a domestic. Some months ago this woman became ill, lost her appetite and conceived the idea that she had been bewitched. She suspected the elder Miss Bartlett of having placed a spell on her and told her so. The girl in a spirit of fun fostered this idea and told the negress she intended prolonging the spell until her victim was dead. Believing in the "Hoodbo" the negress languished for several weeks when finally young Bartlett told her she was the victim of his sister's spirit of mischief. The negress determined to be avenged and awaited her chance until she and Miss Bartlett were alone in the house. T—Traces of precipitation.
TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES.
Charles Cross, a jockey, who was thrown from his horse at the Jerome Park races, on Saturday last, died of his injuries, Sunday night, at the Manhattan Hospital.

A dispatch from Longview, Tex., says that late on Saturday night, nine miles south of that place, in a difficulty about a trivial matter, Walter Rosson, aged eighteen, shot and killed Fletcher Welch, an old man.

A dispatch from Locke, N. Y., says Minnie Mosher, aged sixteen years, was accidently shot in the neck and instantly killed by her twelve-year-old brother, yesterday. The boy was playing with a gun, which he did not know was loaded.

Mrs. Garfield, widow of the late President, has informed the committee of the Grand Army encampment that she will not likely be able to accept the invitation to attend the Grand Army encampment, at Columbus, the first week in September.

Robertson, a negro soldier at Fort Shaw, M. T., on Saturday night had a row with a man near the fort over a sporting woman, and killed an innocent by-stander. Fifty masked citizens from Sun River took the murderer out, Sunday night, and lynched him.

A meeting of Americans who sympathize with the Irish in their struggle to obtain home rule was held at Philadelphia yesterday. Resolutions of greeting to and continued sympathy with Gladstone and Parnell were cabled to them, and $5,500 was raised for the cause of Irish home rule.

Ex-Treasurer Harry C. Carter, of St. Joseph, Mo., has been discovered to be about $8,000 short in his books, and has turned over his property to his bondsmen. The discovery was made in an attempt to make a settlement. Carter claims that the shortage is due to a mistake in making entries.

A boat containing five men was upset near Vinal Haven, Me., on Sunday, and four of them drowned. The party consisted of John Smith, aged thirty-six; Harry Smith, twenty-five; William J. Bishop, twenty-two; Edward Fellows, twenty-six, and George Grant, twenty-five. Grant was the only one saved.

On Sunday the body of one Brysson, riddled with bullets, was found a few miles below Dardanelle, Ark., in the Arkansas river. A few days ago Brysson attempted to criminally assault the wife of Dock Shinn, and was pursued by a posse. It is supposed he was overtaken, shot, and his body flung in the river.

Ex-Sheriff Benjamin F. Van Camp, of Carlton, Orleans county, New York, who had been cited to appear before Surrogate Signor yesterday, to account for moneys received as executor of the Amos Kelsey estate, which amounts to $10,000, did not appear in court, and his whereabouts is unknown. He is executor of several other unsettled estates, and it is supposed he has decamped, leaving an indebtedness which will amount from $20,000 to $25,000.
brysson-1888-06.A3:
FOUND IN THE RIVER.
St. Louis, Mo., June 11.—A special to the Post-Dispatch from Dardanelle, Ark., says: Yesterday the body of one Brison, riddled with bullets, was found a few miles from here in the Arkansas river. A few days ago Brison attempted to criminally assault the wife of Dick Shinn and was pursued by a posse. It is supposed he was overtaken, shot and his body flung in the river.
brysson-1888-06.A5:
Decapitated His Son. WATERLOO, Ia., June 12.—Word has just been received of a tragedy that occurred in Hazel Green township, about seventeen miles from Monticello. An old man by the name of Rothbacker, who was working in a stone quarry with another man, undertook to whip his son, a lad about 12 years of age, when the other man interfered. In the evening the old man tried to whip the boy again, but he ran away. This enraged the father, and he caught the boy, knocked him down and cut his head off with an ax. The officers have been unable to find him. If Rothbacker is caught he will undoubtedly be hung by a mob. A Husband's Terrible Revenge. LITTLE ROCK, Ark., June 12.—One day last week a man named Bryson assaulted the wife of Dr. Shinn. The latter, who lives on the Arkansas river, in Yell county, organized a posse and caught Bryson. The posse returned without him, however, and gave no explanation of his whereabouts. His body was found in the river. It was riddled with bullets and weights were attached to the feet.

SOUTH CAROLINA. people's bank of Darlingto

creased its stock to $200,000.

The deadlock in the third judicial circuit has been broken by the nomination of Mr. Wilson for solicitor.

The Gaffney City Manufacturing Company filed its declaration Friday, and a commission was issued. Capital stock $200,-000.

A shooting affray occurred Tuesday in the lower portion of Laurens county among negroes at a church, in which one was fatally shot.

A. C. Hayes, an energetic farmer of Little Rock, on Oct. 8, lost by fire his barn, containing g.7,000 pounds of oats and fifteen bales of cotton. No insurance.

A colored infant, born dead at Clifton, was exhibited at Laurensville Tuesday. It has two well developed bodies, which join at the breast, but only one head.

On Oct. 18, a delegation from Darlington lodge of the Knights of Pythias will go to Manning to organize a lodge and install the officers. A number of visiting brethren from the various lodges in the state will be present.

The gin house of Mike Still, in Barnwell county, was destroyed by fire on the night of Oct. 3. A large quantity of seed cotton was destroyed, James Still, in trying to extinguish the fire, was severely burned about the face and hands. No insurance.

William Davenport, a character very well known in Greenville as a beggar and morphine slave, died Saturday. He was convicted at Anderson many years ago for the murder of John W. Masks, in Anderson county, in 1865, and was sentenced to be hanged, but was pardoned by Moses.

At Orangeburg, Tuesday, Fred Livingston, who was stricken with paralysis, died at his home. He leaves quite a large family. His life had been insured for $2,000 up to September, when he stopped the payment of the premiums and the policy lapsed. Had he paid $4 more his family would have received $2,000.

At Orangeburg, at a recent meeting of the city board of equalization of the assessment of real estate, a prominent citizen appeared and claimed that a piece of his property was valued too highly, and said he would take for it the amount at which it had been valued, viz.: $1,500. An alderman present said he would give that much cash for it. The citizen accepted, and the sale has since been completed, and both parties well pleased.

H. L. Whitlock, who lives about seven miles west of Lake City, had his dwelling and its contents, together with a 3-year-old child, consumed by fire Thursday. Mr. Whitlock was not at home, and his wife was in the field near the house picking cotton, when she discovered, the house on fire. She ran, but only reached the house in time to see the roof tumble in on the child and hear its pitiful cries for help. She made a desperate effort to rescue the child, but to no avail.

Sheriff Sally has returned to Orangeburg from his trip in Barnwell county, where he went to arrest McFail, Richardson and Crumpler, charged with the killing of Caesar Stephens, colored, at Branchville on the 8th inst. He was unable to find them, but from information received he thinks they will come in and surrender. A Triple Tragedy.

ANNISTON, Ala., October 8.—[Special.]—A triple tragedy took place, this time about half past 3 o'clock. Mr. S. G. Lawrence, a recently elected justice of the peace of this city, accompanied by Will Lacey, his friend and room mate, who was intoxicated, both armed, entered the Hot Blast office for the purpose of making W. H. Edmunds, the editor, retract something he said in a card to the Montgomery Advertiser, denying statements made by Lawrence as correspondent of the Montgomery Dispatch, concerning the difficulty between Edmonds and ex-Policeman Phinize last Monday, which he (Edmonds) declined to do. Lacey, his pal, commenced firing promiscuously a self-cocking revolver, striking Edmonds in the left arm, badly crushing and breaking it. Mr. S. C. Tripney, a plumber of this city, who was in the room, received a ball in the back of the head, coming out through the mouth. John Chappell, a young man connected with the office, was shot through the back of the neck. None of the wounds will likely prove fatal,
Mr. Edmonds may lose his arm. All this has grown out of the war begun a few days ago on the blind tigers. Excitement is running high here with the better class of citizens. A movement will be put on foot to rid the city of such lawlessness. Lacey and Lawrence are in jail.

Killed His Father.

RALEIGH, N. C., October 8.—[Special.]—News was received today that on Saturday afternoon, in Alamance county, a young white man named Rippley shot and instantly killed his father. Three weeks ago a relative died and left young Rippley considerable property and he had been on a spree ever since. Saturday he went to his father's house, and turned his horse into his father's cornfield. His father expostulated. The son became violently angry, and cried out:

"Wait until I come back and I will fix you."

In a little while young Rippley returned with a shot-gun, which he pointed at his father. The father was not frightened.

"You can't scare me in that way."

In an instant he fell dead, shot through the heart. His son had fired both barrels, aiming directly at his breast. The murderer rode to town, and gave himself up to the sheriff, holding out his hands in readiness for the handcuffs.

A Colored Laborer Brutally Murdered.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., October 8.—[Special]—At Mount Pinson, fifteen miles north of this city, on the Mineral railroad, this afternoon, John McCondor, a colored laborer, was brutally murdered by Isaiah Burse, assisted by three other negroes, whose names could not be learned. Burse formerly lived with a negro woman named Lula Davis, but she left him to live with McCondor, who recently married her. While McCondor and his wife were in the waiting-room of the Mount Pinson depot this afternoon, Burse and three other negroes entered without a word. They took McCondor fifty yards from the depot, where Burse shot him three times, killing him instantly. The four negroes then fled and have not been captured. After the killing McCondor's wife went to his body, took all the money in his pockets and then she, too, fled to the woods.

Her Life Spared.

RALLEIGH, N. C., October 9.—[Special.]

Governor Scales to-day commuted to life imprisonment the death sentence of Cora Wright, colored, who was to be hanged at Tarboro November 2. She was convicted of murdering her six months old child by placing it in a hollow stump and letting it starve to death. Her accomplice in this crime was a negro man. But for him she would have relented and spared the child. She was used as evidence against her accomplice, who will be hanged November 2d.

For this reason, and because she is evidently of weak mind, the governor commutes the sentence. The application for commutation was signed by the judge, jury and solicitor. No application has been made for the commutation of the death sentence of Millie Potetate, the negro woman who is to be hanged at Yanceyville next Friday.

An Incendiary Fire.

PORTLAND, Ogn., October 9.—A fire broke out in Moscow, Idaho, this morning, destroying a number of buildings. The loss is $70,000. The fire was evidently incendiary. The Moscow city council recently passed an ordinance excluding gamblers and thieves, and threats had been made by them against the town. It is believed that this fire is the result.

Shot Down by Three Men.

CHARLESTON, S. C., October 10.—[Special.]

News has reached here of a most brutal and outrageous murder committed near Branchville, in this state. The victim was Caesar Stevens, an inoffensive negro. His murderers, McFall, Crumpler and Richardson, three white men, accompanied by others, entered a garden in which Stevens was at work and shot the man down in cold blood, literally riddling him with bullets and shot, after which they deliberately rode away. They made no attempt to hide their identity. The cause for the murder is not known. It was not politics, for the victim was well known and liked by

A Negro Killed at Branchville.
BRANCHVILLE, Oct. 9.—A negro was was brutally murdered here yesterday. It was an outrageous affair, and reminded one of the murders perpetrated by the cowboys on the frontiers of Texas. The facts are about as follows: Caesar Stevens, the deceased, who was in the employ of Mr. A. F, H. Dukes, got into a difficulty with another negro on Saturday last, who was driving a wagon for some folks from the country.

Mr. A. F. H. Dukes succeeded in quieting these two negroes, but some white men, the friends of the country negro, renewed the quarrel with Caesar and threatened to kill him. These men finally left here on Saturday night, but returned yesterday morning, fully armed with pistols and a shotgun. They found the deceased peaceably at work in Mr. Dukes's garden and immediately opened fire on him, shooting at him at least twelve or fifteen times and striking him in nine places.

The three men who did the shooting were W. L. McFail, T. S. Crumpler and J. A. Richardson. There were several others who were here as accessories. The negro lingered until 8 o'clock this morning when he died. The murderers as yet have not been arrested.

The universal opinion of the town is that it was a most cold-blooded and outrageous murder, and that the parties ought to be puuished to the full extent of the law. The deceased was a quiet, inoffensive negro, and well thought of by both white and black.—Special to News and Courier.

Thomas Stack Declares That It Was Neither His Son's Nor His Son's Wife's, Though It Figures as Their Child.

A suit has been begun recently in the Court of Common Pleas in this city which involves the conception of an extraordinary and romantic conspiracy. Thomas Stack of Brooklyn is the complainant. He was once a great shipbuilder and worth a million. Misfortune has reduced his fortune considerably, though he is by no means a poor man to-day. The suit is brought in equity to secure possession of an estate worth somewhat more than $100,000, the value of property bequeathed to Mr. Stack's son Daniel by his grandfather. Originally this estate was worth about $52,000, and according to the provisions of Grandfather Stack's will, the income from it was to be equally divided between Daniel and his sister during their lives. In the event of the death of one of them the whole income was to be paid to the other. If one or both of them left issue, the whole estate was to be transferred absolutely to these children per capita. If both died without issue, the estate was to be divided between various other members of the family, of whom Thomas Stack, the complainant, is the only survivor.

With this complex arrangement properly included in his will, all signed and sealed and placed in safe keeping. Grandfather Stack probably died happy in the belief that he had provided against litigation over his bequests.

Grandson Stack, according to common report, was feeble minded, and, according to his father's complaint in this suit, he was imbecile and physically incompetent. Nevertheless, on May 7, 1878, he was married to Eva L. Mischwitz. His sister having died, he received the whole benefit of the income derived from his grandfather's bequest. Five years after his marriage, which was without issue, his wife secured a decree of absolute divorce, the co-respondent being Emma M. Johnson. Some time after the divorce Mrs. Stack married again, and has had children by her present husband.

On March 25, 1883, prior to the divorce, the Johnson woman, with whom Daniel Stack was living, presented to him a baby which she said was his. This child has since died. As soon as the decree of divorce was pronounced Daniel was taken by Mrs. Johnson to Sound Beach, Connecticut, where, it is alleged, she kept him in seclusion, his father never being able to see him. During this time, acting on legal advice, she went to Philadelphia with Daniel, and there they were married. Even after that Thomas Stack knew nothing of his son's condition until he received a telegram summoning him to Sound Beach. When he arrived Daniel was dead.

The second Mrs. Stack was eventually married to a man named Pike, by whom she has had no children. In the course of time Mrs. Pike propounded a document to the Surrogate which she alleged to be the last will and testament of Daniel Stack, in which she is named as the sole executor of the estate. Thomas Stack filed several objections to the probate of this will, questioning first the legality of his son's second marriage and therefore the legitimacy of the child, and alleging that this child was not only fraudulently foisted upon Daniel, but that it was not even the child of Mrs. Emma M. Stack, now Pike. The Surrogate cited Supreme Court decisions sustaining the legality of the marriage, but he permitted Mr. Stack to attack the marriage and prove, if he could, that it had been without issue. This could not be done in the Surrogate's Court, hence the present action in the Court of Common Pleas.

It will be seen, if this legal problem is carefully inspected, that in order to obtain possession of Daniel's $100,000 it was necessary that he should have had issue, and his natural heir having died, the property would fall by the terms of his will to his second wife. Whether Mrs. Pike actually plotted to secure a fortune in this way remains to be proven, but Thomas Stack attempts to prove it, incidentally attacking his son's testamentary capacity.

The other side denies all these allegations, and expects to disprove them.

CANNIBALISTIC PAYTON.
The Man Who Shot Crookston's Chief of Police Eats His Own Flesh.
CROOKSTON, Minn., Dec. 14.—A larger number of criminal cases is on the calendar at the term of court now in session here than has ever been known before. To-day B. F. Clayton was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary for horse stealing and A. O. Hanson was given two years for burglary. James Payton, the man who shot Chief of Police Hayes, was convicted of assault with intent to kill, and was returned to jail to await sentence. Upon being placed in his cell Payton attempted to beat his brains out against the iron bars, and had to be tied to the floor. This made him so furious that he tore the flesh completely from both arms with his teeth in attempts to free himself. His arms are in a frightful condition, the muscles and bones being left bare and the flesh being fearfully mangled.

SUNDAY a negro named Doe Moran wrote a note requesting a correspondence with Miss Lizzie Shackleford, a most worthy young lady, and stuck it where she was sure to find it. Highly incensed she took it to Mr. William Daugherty, who immediately set a trap for the rascal. He got Marshal Newland and stationed him where he could not be seen and when the negro came for the answer, which he requested should be left in the same place, Newland brought his gun down and took him in. Mr. Daugherty was so outraged that he was with difficulty restrained from shooting the scamp, who begged most pitcously for mercy. He was brought down town and threats of lynching scared him so he could hardly stand on his feet. A proposition to hit him 1,000 on his naked back met with his warmest approval, but it was finally agreed that if he would strike for tall timber and never show himself here again, he could go and he stood not upon its order, but let out at once. If he is ever caught here again he will repent his rashness.

DEADLY WORK WITH THE PISTOL.
One Police Officer Fatally Shoots Another, and Wounds Several Bystanders.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal

ELKKART, Ind., Oct 27.—Officer William Burton, an old and highly respected police officer of this city, was shot, this afternoon at 3 o'clock, by officer Joseph Barrett, another old officer, while several others had narrow escapes. The causes leading to the occurrence are as follows: A short time ago, Mayor Goldthwait officially reprimanded Barrett for continued intoxication, and the matter so preyed on the latter's mind that, last night, he waylaid the Mayor and very severely whipped him. For this offense he was placed under bonds to the amount of $1,000 to appear at the Circuit Court and, failing in securing a bondsman and becoming partially intoxicated, he drew a revolver, this afternoon, and threatened to shoot officer Sutton when the latter undertook to arrest him, but was dissuaded from doing so by his wife. A few minutes later he was met by Marshal Needham and officer Burton, and when they undertook to arrest him quietly he threatened to shoot, and when Burton grasped him from behind Barrett discharged his revolver, the ball striking a horse in the knee. He fired again, the ball striking Burton back of the left eye, passing clear through his head, and causing instant death. A third shot took off the end of one of Councilman Stears's fingers while the latter was struggling with him. A fourth grazed Needham's head, partially stunning him, and the fifth and last passed through another man's hat Needham and Councilman Wagner then fired several shots at the infuriated man, but it is not known that he was hit, though he claimed to be shot in the groin. At this point Sheriff Chatten overpowered Barrett, forced him into a saloon and fastened the door, while the enraged mob procured a rope and endeavored to get at the murderer to lynch him. Mayor Goldthwait and Sheriff Chatten addressed the crowd, and succeeded in quieting it, somewhat, but fortunately a heavy rain-storm came up and dispersed the gathering, and before it could come together again Barrett was placed in a carriage and driven to the county jail at Goshen, where he arrived safe. Burton was about thirty-five years of age, a giant in size, and has a wife and young family. Barrett also has a family and has been considered a good officer.

BLOODTHIRSTY BARRETT.
A Hoosier Policeman Kills a Brother Officer and Wounds Several Others.
eral Others.

ELKHART, Ind., Oct. 27.—Police Officer Joseph Barrett this afternoon shot and instantly killed a brother officer named William Burton. Barrett had been on the force for several years, but yesterday Mayor Goldwaith reprimanded him for drunkenness. Last night, in a spirit of revenge, he waylaid the mayor and gave him a severe whipping. This morning he was bound over in bonds and after the trial an attempt was made to arrest him on a new charge. This he resisted, and pulling his revolver he began to empty it. The second shot pierced Burton's brain, and the succeeding three shots wounded as many bystanders. The man then took refuge in a saloon, and the citizens at once began to take steps which looked towards his lynching, but the prompt interference of the mayor and other policemen, saved his life. He was at once taken to Goshen for safe keeping. One of the shots tore off the finger of a city alderman.
elkhart-elkhart-1888-10.A6:
NEWS IN SHORT ORDER.
DOMESTIC HAPPENINGS TOLD IN A FEW BRIEF WORDS.
Interesting Paragraphs Condensed from Many Redundant Columns.
The Berkshire Woolen, Company of Great Barrington, Mass., failed. The capital stock is $100,000. Assets and liabilities unknown.

Isadore Meyer and Gillaume Ladore of Helena, Mon., who sailed from Stubb's Ferry for a trip up the Missouri, have not been heard from, and it is feared they have been drowned.

Carl Shekelman of Columbus, Ind., who has just returned from a tour of Central Africa, has brought home with him a 9 year old negro prince, whose father is king of the Lonagan country. The prince is uncivilized.

The murder of a policeman on duty in Elkhart, Ind., by one just dismissed from the force for drunkenness, has roused the people to the point of attacking the jail to lynch the murderer.

Policeman James Brennan, of New York, was shot and killed by Henry Carlton, an exconvict, known to the police as "Handsome Harry." Carlton was seeking to avoid arrest.

Mary Crocker, 18 years of age, of Barnstable, Mass., died of hydrophobia resulting from a bite by a pet dog a year ago.

John Keegan, of Scranton, Pa., convicted of killing Mrs. Patrick Bartlett, was sentenced to twelve years in the penitentiary.

A man, supposed to be P. Hartmann of Harrodsburg, Ky., committed suicide at the main door of the Centennial Exposition at Cincinnati by cutting his throat.

Yellow fever is decreasing in Jacksonville, but on the increase in Southern Florida.

A legacy to be divided between two brothers at Brellam, Ark., caused a quarrel in which one of them stabbed the other, inflicting mortal wounds.

A special from Kansas City, Mo., says that two freight trains on the Chicago, St. Paul and Milwaukee road collided at Minneville, a small station north of there. Two firemen and two brakemen were killed. Both of the trains were badly wrecked.

Fireman Charles Baun and Engineer Foote were killed in a collision near San Jose, Ill.

Louis Bittner committed suicide in Louisville by shooting himself.

—Captain Simpson, of the steamship Escalona, fell overboard at St. John, N. B., and was drowned.

—The jury investigating the death by burning of young Thomas F. Dalton, aged 19, of St. Louis, returned a verdict that he came to his death by his mother, pouring burning oil over deceased's clothing and setting fire thereto. The mother was intoxicated when the crime was committed, and had quarreled with her son.

—The Rev. Robert Eckles, a Methodist minister, was killed by a train in Reno, Pa., while crossing the track.

—The Union Palace Car Company, with a capital of $3,000,000, has been organized in opposition to the Pullman Company.

—The Grand Jury at Provo City, Utah, found 234 indictments for offences that grew out of the practice of polygamy.

—Croton oil was put into the soup at a communion service of Dunkards in Huntington county, Ind., and of the participants at the service three will probably die.

—The Coroner's Jury has decided that Conductor Bowman and Engineer Fuller are responsible for the accident near Shippensburg, Pa., where one man was killed and fifteen persons injured.

—Sylvester Grubb, who shot and killed his sweetheart on the Princeton fair grounds, Vincennes, Ind., last September, was sentenced to be hanged April 19. He received his sentence without betraying any emotion.

—The last spike of the St. Paul, Minneapolis and Manitoba system was driven in Sioux Falls, Dak., amid shrieking of whistles, ringing of bells and booming of cannon. The road will be known as the Wilmar and Sioux Falls road. It has cost Sioux Falls $65,000 and is the seventh line entering the city.

—At a meeting in Paris of the Republican Left of the Senate it was shown that the majority of the members of the Senate were opposed to Premier Flouquet's proposal for the revision of the Constitution. They consider the scheme to be fraught with danger to parliamentary power, and at the same time to the liberty of action of the Executive.

—Peter Commisky, an employee of the Canadian Pacific Railroad at Greenville, Me., was literally blown to pieces by the explosion of two large caps of fulminating powder. He was holding them in his hand, when a spark from a forge ignited them.

—The 12,000 coke workers in the Connelsville region were notified of an advance of from 5 to 10 per cent. in their wages, to take effect on Nov. 1, when the price of coke will be advanced 25 cents per ton, in accordance with the agreement made by the operators.

—David Veatar, a barkeeper, shot his wife and himself at Colfax, W. T. Both died almost instantly.

—The Brotherhood of Railway Brakemen, which has been in session at Columbus, Ohio, adjourned. The federation scheme was dropped.

—A passenger train on the Fitchburg road telescoped a freight train which was standing on the track just below Eagle Bridge station. Engineer Vandervoort of the passenger train sustained a broken nose and serious internal injuries, and Conductor Gray was also hurt. Not a passenger was injured. The locomotive of the passenger train was wrecked, as was also the caboose of the freight.

—Maggie Watts, colored, aged 24 years, was arrested in Providence. She is wanted in New Bedford for drawing a pistol on a school teacher, who had refused to allow her brother to leave school on her demand.

—As a result of "Old Hutch's" grip on the wheat market, the exportation of wheat from the port of Boston has fallen off from 16 cargoes, consisting of 409,858 bushels, in September, to 4 cargoes, comprising 55,077 bushels, thus far this month.

—In Ansonia, Ct., while 16-year-old Patrick Crowley, a newsboy, was gathering chestnuts in Wallace's grove, a tree was blown down, striking him square on the head, crushing his skull and killing him instantly.

—For years the Isthmus of Panama has been a "quack's paradise." At last the Government has grappled with the evil. Heavy fines or imprisonment are provided for the first three offences of practicing medicine, surgery, or pharmacy without being duly qualified, and the fourth offence is punishable by expulsion from the Republic.

—James Clancey, of Chicago, went into his barn to feed his horse after dark. The horse bit his nose off. Clancey tried to get to the nearest drug store, but fell from loss or blood before reaching there. He is in some danger of blood poisoning.

—The residence, and furniture store of Charles Nigabower, in Ilion, N. Y., were burned. Nigabower and his daughter, aged twelve years, perished in the flames. The girl had rescued a younger brother and gone back.

—While Joaquin Miller was shooting quail, his horse jumped unexpectedly, and a bullet went through his left hand, making a painful flesh wound. The only danger is from lock-jaw.

—Col. W. C. Forry, United States Swamp Land Commissioner, was arrested at Iowa Falls and taken to Eldora charged with treating a personal friend to a drink of whiskey. He admitted it and was fined $100 and costs by Mayor Ward.

NOTES FROM UNION COUNTY.
ETTA JANE, August 25.—Illegibility on our part, or an oversight of the compositor, dates our last letter "August 26." Also, "1887" occurs in the same communication instead of 1877, the date we intended. That was the best crop year this county has had in 15 years. We have noted an abundant oat crop in 1882.

On his farm, last Thursday, Mr. Jonathan Buice killed the largest "upland moccasin" we have seen in many years, if ever, before. It would measure nearly 4 feet in length and was as large around its body as a common man's arm.

Last Tuesday was remarkably windy. The corn blades were in many places riddled into strings. Since then the thermometer has gone down several degrees and vegetation, especially cotton, shows its effect.

The campaign in this county, so far as we know is practically at an end, and if reports are worth believing, a more corrupt measure has never been carried through in a "Primary." No political issue of any importance was before the people to engender the strife that was exhibited on that occasion; but the reports circulated about the different candidates during the campaign, and especially just before the election, were truly disgusting. The philosophical and honest statesmen are bound to admit that fair elections in this country are not to be expected in every instance. We are not chagrined at the result, but we merely give our observation from our standpoint. We like to see "brethren dwell together in unity."

Farmers are having fine weather to pull fodder and most of them are at it.

Our railroad cat is expected to jump some time before long, but we can find no one who knows where she will alight on the Three C's. At present her feline optics are on Hickory Grove. We have long since learned that railroad or other moneyed corporations are like the old man who took his wife to assist him in selecting a place to build his house. He said to her: "Honey, you can have it built just where you please; but I'm going to have it right here." SIGMA.

STATE POLITICAL ITEMS.

— Some people over in Orangeburg have been exercised over a report that John Peter Richardson went a fishing on Sunday. They have doubtless mistaken the Governor for Simon Peter, who was a fisherman and a very good man, too, but who died over eighteen centuries ago. [Barnwell People.

— The Hon. J. J. Hemphill was renominated, without opposition, to Congress at the Congressional Convention held at Yorkville on the 15th. This will make his fourth term, and it will be better to send him to Congress several times four terms if he continues to do as well as heretofore. [Cheraw Reporter.

— The opposition in this county to Governor Richardson is not of a personal character, but because of his indifference to the establishment of an agricultural college. Personally he is very popular with all who know him, but duty many times compel men to vote against candidates who may be their personal friends and favorites. [Orangeburg Times and Democrat.

— The people of the Sixth Congressional District have made a great mistake in the renomination of a godless man, in the person of G. W. Dargan, to Congress. It is a stigma upon the Christianity of this State that such a man, who is known to be an agnostic, should represent a God-fearing people in any capacity. It would have been far better to have no representative at all than one who will misrepresent the dearest convictions of the heart of a noble people. We cannot afford to insult God even in politics. Retribution will follow. Come it will, and in this instance, too. Mark it, people of the Sixth Congressional District!—Sumter Watchman.

Several of the counties have elected anti-Richardson delegates to the State Convention. While there will not be enough, perhaps, to prevent his nomination on the first ballot, there seems to be in many places a decided desire for another man. This feeling arises from the fact that the offices belong to the people and not to the man. When a whole State ticket unites in their demand for a second term because they have done well the first, it looks to the average voter like a sort of close corporation affair. That is about the secret of the opposition to Governor Richardson. Many of the people feel that he belongs to the office-holders and not to the people, hence they prefer a new man fresh from the ranks and more in sympathy with them than the body of office-holders in the State.—Carolina Spartan.

SOUTH CAROLINA NEWS.

A special dispatch to the Charleston World conveys the information that on Thursday James Stokes and his family, of Orangeburg, were poisoned, Mr. Stokes fatally, by eating ice cream.

The department of agriculture has decided to make a State exhibit at the Augusta exposition. It is expected to make as good a showing as at New Orleans, and every one having any fine products is desired to send the same to Commissioner Butler.

Mr. George D. McCants, a prominent citizen of Winnsboro, died Thursday at Shelby, N. C., from a stroke of paralysis. Mr. McCants had been sick for some time, suffering from Bright's disease, and had visited Cleveland Springs and Shelby in the hope of benefiting his health. He was 43 years old, but left no family.

The mill belonging to Mrs. M. A. Self, near Limestone, Edgefield county, was blown up last Tuesday by an explosion of the boiler. It resulted in the death of two negroes, one dying in the morning and the other the evening following, and completely demolished the whole building, blowing the mill stones some twenty feet or more.

The South Carolina railroad commissioners have inspected the Georgia, Carolina and Northern road, which is now completed from Monroe, N. C., to Fishing Creek, twelve miles from Chester. They completed their inspection Thursday and opened the road according to the laws of the State. The work on the road will be delayed at Fishing Creek a few days on account of the construction of a bridge, but Chester will be reached by September 15th.

On the 13th of August, Wade H. Suber, who lived with Abraham Moore, near Prosperity, Newberry county, took a bale of cotton to that town, sold it and started ostensibly for home in the wagon in which the cotton was sold. Suber, however, did not return to his home. The driver, a negro, stated when he got home that he had left Mr. Suber in town. Upon further inquiry the negro stated that Mr. Suber would not come home; that he had gone off with the money for the bale of cotton, which belonged to Mr. Moore. The family suspected as much, and for several days kept the matter quiet. While Suber's neighbors were accusing the negro of having murdered and robbed him, and were entertaining serious intentions of lynching the darkey, Suber was discovered to be alive and well at Spartanburg.

INSTALLATION OF A PASTOR.—On Friday evening last, at the regular hour of worship, Rev. C. E. Todd was installed as pastor of the Associate Reformed Presbyterian church in Charlotte, N. C. Rev. R. G. White preached the sermon; Rev. C. E. McDonald charged the pastor, and Rev. J. C. Galloway charged the congregation.

O'NEILL, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—The funeral of Mrs. Wilcox, who was killed on Tuesday by the accidental discharge of a revolver in the hands of her husband, took place yesterday at 2 o'clock from the Presbyterian church, Rev. J. A. Abbott officiating. She was buried under the auspices of the order of Odd Fellows, of which she had taken the Rebecca degree. A large concourse of friends and relatives followed the remains to the grave. A. L. Wilcox, the husband, was arrested to-day on complaint of Robert Earl, son of Mrs. Wilcox by a former husband, on the charge of willful and deliberate murder. The accused was arraigned before Judge Lowe at 3 o'clock and plead not guilty. The case was continued until Tuesday morning at 10 o'clock. The prisoner is in charge of an officer. Holt County's Institute.

O'NEILL, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—To-day practically closed a two weeks' session of the Holt county normal school, which, under the efficient management of Superintendent Manville and the excellent instruction of Profs. Bond of Blair, Viefs of Texas and Bland of O'Neill, has been the best ever held in Holt county. Two hundred and two members have enrolled and the interest of all connected with the institute has been very marked. State Superintendent Lane was here Monday but was called home to the sick bed of some member of his family. To-morrow at noon the normal formally closes.

Heat His Daughter Brutally.

NEBRASKA CITY, Neb., August 3 — [Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Georce Ostrander, a painter, was arrested and jailed to-night for beating his sixteen-year-old daughter into unconsciousness, and leaving her body and head a mass of bruises. Neighbors interfered and cared for the girl, or he would doubtless have killed her. When arrested there were cries for "a rope" by a mob assembled, and had not the officers hustled Ostrander off he would have been roughly handled. He says the cause for the beating is that the daughter and mother were too conspicuous upon the streets after night.

Whitman Gets the County Seat.

WHITMAN, Neb., August 2.—[Special to THE BEE.]—A special election held in Grant county on the 21st of July resulted in the county seat being located at Whitman by about half a dozen majority. The following named persons were elected county officers: K. M. Moran, sheriff; Sidney Manning, clerk; George Collins, judge; Milton Dodds, treasurer; O. P. Warner, attorney; William L. Hall, superintendent of schools; Augustus Bufinke, George Swiggart, Thomas Lynch, commissioners.

They Wouldn't Believe Him.

NEBRASKA CITY, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Henry Meyers, at whose house the murderous row took place several days ago, and who was arrested under the Slocumb law relating to giving away liquors on Sunday, was to-day found not guilty by a jury and discharged by Justice Jones, after Meyers had acknowledged the truth of the charges.

A Needed Rain.

O'NEILL, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A wind storm came up this afternoon about 4 o'clock, accompanied by a little hail and followed by a good rain. This assures a good crop of corn in the belt reached by the rain. The harvesting of small grain is in full blast and good returns are promised.

Voted Court House Bonds.

BREWSTER, Neb., August 3.—[Special Tel-

Voted Court House Bonds.
BREWSTER, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Five thousand dollar bonds to build a court house and fund the indebtedness carried yesterday by a small majority. Only a small vote was polled. Dunning precinct beat her past record, polling forty-seven votes against the bonds and three for.
Wind and Rain in Nuckolls County.
NELSON, Neb., August 3.—[Special Tele]

Wind and Rain in Nuckolls County.
NELSON, Neb., August 3.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A heavy wind this afternoon blew the cornice from the new National bank building. The falling brick missed H. W. Malone by a few inches. Sufficient rain fell to save corn, but strips of hail did some damage also.

Congressman Dorsey's Return.
FREMONT, Neb., August 3.—[Special to THE BEE.]—Congressman Dorsey arrived home yesterday from Washington. He will remain here a few days, after which, in company with Mrs. Dorsey, he will make a pleasure trip through Lake Superior.

Nominated for Congress.
St. Louis, August 3.—The democrats of the Twentieth Illinois district, in convention at Murphysboro, nominated T. T. Robiuson, of Jackson, for congress.

Killed by a Cable Car.
St. Paul, August 3.—Corporal Fird, Third infantry, from Fort Snelling, in attempting to board a cable car last evening, fell under the car and was killed.

WHILE bathing in the Elkhorn river at West Point the other day Ernest Boettcher, a German farmer, aged twenty-one years, was drowned.

By a late wreck on the Omaha & Republican Valley railroad, a quarter of a mile north of Upton, six tramps were killed. Four of the bodies were identified by papers on their persons as George Stokes, residence unknown; John Gleason, Earl Talbott, a boy of about twenty, apparently a German, with letters addressed to him at Columbus, Neb.: John C. Taylor, Louisville, Ky., with a letter from his wife Kate. Two cars were derailed, one loaded with shelled corn, in which were the six tramps. The car rolled down an embankment about fifteen feet and came to a stand still bottom side up, and the unfortunate men, who were stealing a ride, were smothered under the corn.

A large barn on the farm of J. P. Dunlap, at Dwight, caught fire and was burned the other day. It was supposed that the fire was started from an engine on the Fremont, Elkhorn & Missouri Valley railroad. Loss about $2,000, with small insurance.

The other night as a young man by the name of Schmidt, his sister and two brothers named Vandoschmiet were returning from a wedding in Ewing a row commenced in which Schmidt was fatally stabbed in the abdomen, his sister cut across the arm, one of the Vandoschmiets had a shoulder broken and was stabbed twice in the back and the other Vandoschmiet seriously injured about the head. Schmidt's injuries were fatal.

Emmons, the murderer of Bertha Schultz, was taken from jail at Pawnee City by a mob about three o'clock the other morning and hanged from the Chicago, Kansas & Nebraska bridge. Emmons killed the girl because she refused to marry him. He had been a Methodist evangelist and a railway well digger. He was twenty-five years old and the girl twenty. He shammed insanity after his arrest and pretended that he had no recollection of murdering the girl.

The premium list of the annual fair of the Chase County agricultural society has just been issued. The fair will be held at Imperial September 4, 5, 6 and 7. Premiums to the amount of $1,717 are offered.

It is predicted that 200 students will attend the fall term of Hastings College.

Dr. T. L. Myers, a prominent physician of Aurora, attempted to board a freight train at Bromfield the other night, and fell under the wheels. His head was severed from his body.

Some weeks ago three men broke into the Acme mill at Blair, beat the engineer, G. W. Fackler, in a brutal manner and helped themselves to all the flour they could carry away. The other morning about two o'clock Fackler heard a noise in the store room and found three men there helping themselves. He opened fire with his revolver and one of the men with a groan fell to the floor. His two companions, who had jumped outside the window, sprang back and picking the wounded man up carried him away. They were traced some distance by the blood but finally escaped.

Chris Robidou, a young bully living near Norden, assaulted an old man named Samuels the other day because the latter protested against his driving over a garden patch. Robidou was not satisfied with a couple of knock-downs, but started to finish the old man with an axe, when neighbors interfered. Samuels is over seventy years old, and the neighbors were about to treat his assailant with a coat of tar and feathers when Robidou made his escape.

Cora, the daughter of A. L. Wilcox, of O'Neill, recently eloped with and married a man objectionable to her parents and who had made threats against Mrs. Wilcox. Mr. Wilcox having occasion to leave home bought a pistol for his wife to defend herself with in case of emergency. The other morning they rose early and when he was ready to start Mr. Wilcox was showing his wife how to use the pistol when it was accidentally discaarged, the ball entering her heart and killing her instantly.

A HAY SPRINGS brute has been given public warning that unless he desists from castigating his little step-son with a rawhide he will be given a big dose of his own medicine.

Ohio soldiers living in the neighborhood of Beatrice are talking of chartering a special car and attending the National G. A. R. reunion at Columbus, O., next September.

The post-office at Superior was struck by lightning the other evening, the fluid performing a number of curious antics, but injuring no one.

The only son of Tom Montgomery, who resides in the northeast corner of Gage County, was drowned in the Blue river, about three miles northeast of Wilber, the other day.

GEORGE OSTRANDER, a painter, was arrested at Nebraska City the other night for beating his sixteen-year-old daughter so badly that her life is in danger. He was followed to jail by a mob yelling for a rope, and had it not been for the care of officers he would have fared badly.

It is reported that when the fast east-bound freight on the Burlington road reached Benkelman the other day the train men put four tramps off the train, and pounded them badly, breaking one man's nose and nearly severing an ear from another. The tramps reported that one of their number was thrown from the train at Park's Station, ten miles west, when the train was running thirty miles an hour. About a week ago young Gibson received a check for several hundred dollars from his father. He cashed it and has not since been seen by his classmates. His father has been informed of the young man's disappearance, and detectives are at work on the case. Killed His Wife in Church.
FULTON, Mo., Oct. 24.—Jackson Emmeron, colored, entered the Pilgrim's Rest church Monday night and, without a word of warning, drew a revolver and fired at his wife, Nina, missing her. A second shot entered the back of her head, coming out over the right eye, and the woman fell over dead. The congregation stampeded and the preacher jumped out of a second-story window. Emmerson is in jail, and there are strong threats of lynching him.

Two Brutes Escape Lynching.

NEW HAVEN, Oct. 24.—George Williams, colored, and Charles Crandall, white, broke into the farm house of Mr. Schorkowski, aged 77 years, near Durham, at 2 oi'clock yesterday morning, knocked the old man senseless and injured his wife, aged 67 years. Two Men Killed in a Smash-Up.

DENVER, Col., Oct. 24.—Report reached here Monday evening that while a freight train was standing on the main track of the Burlington road at Menesaw, Neb., the engine of another freight train crashed into the caboose and completely wrecked the first train and the engine of the second, instantly killing George A. Pritchard of Denver and Robert Bean of Meeker, Cal.

What Soldier's Skeleton is This?

PETERSBURG, Va., Oct. 24.—Monday while tearing up the floor of the kitchen of the Dinwiddie county court house here workmen found the skeleton of a man with a musket and canteen near by. The floor was some distance above ground and the supposition is that the soldier while wounded or sick went under the kitchen and while there died. It is supposed that he was a member of one of the Union regiments that were stationed in this locality.

Gone to Look for Burled Gold.

BOSTON, Oct. 24.—Inspector "Bill" Watts of police headquarters, armed with a pickaxe, a shovel, and a diagram, started Monday for Montreal. It has leaked out that he has gone in search of a pot which was secreted by "Old Joe" Fowle, and which is said to contain $8,000 in gold, the proceeds of Fowle's various swindling operations in this city.

Shot His Sweetheart.

OWENSBORO, Ky., Oct. 24.—Noah Jagoe Monday evening fatally shot Miss Ella Green, to whom he was engaged to be married. He says it was an accident. Miss Green would make no statement. From the fact that he tried to stab her a short time ago and had been quarrelling with her about receiving other company, he is suspected of shooting with intent to kill.

An Aged Middletown Couple Ill-Treated by Two Drunken Ruffians.

Thomas Schorskowski, a native of Poland, who is 77 years old, lives near the Pine Grove cemetery in Middletown on the road to Durham. About 2 a. m. Tuesday his house was broken into by two ruffians, who seized Mrs Schorskowski, carried her out of the house, and the crime of rape was committed by each of the young men, whose names are George Williams and Charles Crandall. Williams is a colored man, and while he was outraging the old lady his white accomplice knocked down the aged husband, who was trying to rescue his wife.

After committing the crime, the assailants fled. The neighbors were notified, and Edwin J. Roberts came into the city to inform the police. Chief Chapman went out about 4 a. m. and, by shrewd detective work captured the criminals at the old Dooley place near the Durham line. They were brought to Middletown and will be examined in the police court to-day if their victims are strong enough to appear against them.

Surgeon Edgerton reports that Mrs Schorskowski, who is 67 years old, was seriously injured. The couple are worthy, and the neighbors speak well of them. It is stated that the criminals were nerved to commit the great crime by a free use of strong drink, and an empty bottle left where the outrage was committed givss color to the statement. Williams and Crandall are wood choppers.

worse than Murdebers.—Mrs. Schor kowski, aged sixty-seven, who lives on a farm near Durham, Conn., was dragged from bed early yesterday morning by two men and brutally outraged. About two o'clock, Mr. and Mrs. Schorkowski were aroused by a noise at their front door. Before they could get up the door was smashed in and two ruffians rushed into the bedroom, seized the old lady and dragged her out to the roadside, where both men outraged her. Geo. Williams, colored, the first offender, held his hand over the old lady's mouth to prevent her from screaming. While Williams was committing the assault, the old lady's husband, who is seventy-seven years old, rushed up to defend her. Charles Crandall, white, the other brute, hit the old man on the head with a club, knocking him senseless. Crandall next assaulted the woman, and then the scoundrels fled, leaving the couple unconscious by the roadside. When the old man recovered he aroused a neighbor, who informed the chief of police who tracked the man to an unfrequented place on the Doo'ey farm, where they were found playing cards in a wood-chopper's shanty. They were quickly handcuffed and taken to Schorkowski's house, where both were fully identified. The horrible character of the case has created intense excitement in the vicinity.

Wretches Found Guilty.
IDDLETOWN. Ct. Oct. 24.—George
Wretches Found Guildy.
MIDDLETOWN, Ct., Oct. 24.—George Williams (colored) and Charles Crandall (white), who were arrested Tuesday afternoon for committing an outrage upon Mrs. Caroline Schorkowski, who lives on the Durham road three miles out, were tried in the police court to-day. The were found guilty and bound over to the November term of the Superior court under bonds of $2,500 each.
Mrs. Schorkowski, who was unable to walk without assistance, appeared against the prisoners and testified to the outrage upon her. The prisoners were taken to Haddam jail this afternoon to await trial.

A True Bill Found.
The grand jury convened in Middletown yesterday and was instructed by Judge Fenn. They retired, organized by choosing A. M. Wright of Essex chairman, and found a true bill against Charles Crandall and George Williams, who are charged with committing rape upon Mrs Schokowski, an aged woman, who lives with her husband on the Durham road. The crime was committed on October 22, and the accused will be tried at the December term of the superior court. The jury was excused until Tuesday, when it will convene again and inquire concerning the killing of Mrs Cooper of Portland, who was murdered by her husband on Monday morning of this week.
