Owl Club, owing to the inclementy of the weather, did not convene on last Monday night, but will hold its meeting next Monday night, with the same program.

Mr. Ira P. Rudolph who is in the hardware business at Arkadelphia, came down last week to see his family and be present at the public installation of the Masonic Lodge No. 80, of which he is a member.

The U. L. P. county convention met at this place last Saturday and nominated the following men for the various county offices: Representative, O. S. Jones; Clerk, J. M. Pittman; Judge, G. A. Robinson; Sheriff, J. S. Beagan; Treasurer, Black; Assessor, J. G. Purifoy; Surveyor, L. E. Melson; Coroner, S. S. Brooks.

A negro named Grant Alexander, assaulted a white lady in Boughton township last week, but was foiled in his hellish intent. He was easily captured and identified, bound over by the examining court and is now in the state penetentiary, for safe keeping. Several attempts were made to lynch him but failed, the jail was surrounded by negroes every night for purpose of protecting him and some measures was felt that the vigilantes and guard would come in conflict.

The Jeffersonian Lyceum met at the school house last Friday night, and discussed the following question: "Resolved, that the ports of the United States should be opened to all kinds of immigration," which resulted in a decision in favor of the negative. It will meet again next Friday night, and discuss whether or not the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors should be prohibited by legislation. All are earnestly required to come out, and thus encourage the young men in their ambitious course.

We hear some severe strictures upon Sheriffs Regan and Greer for having placed a guard about the jail on Saturday night. Whille we believe it ill-advised to have constituted this guard of negroes and to have placed them in an attitude of defying resprettable and outraged white citizens, we commend the officers for their effort to do their duty in the protection of prisoners and county property. Under no circumstances should Judge Lynch be permitted to re-precede established law after legal proceedings have been instituted.

The officers of Masonic Lodge, No. 80, were installed June 25th, at Prescott. The proceedings were opened with prayer by Rev. R. M. Traylor; after which Mr. D. C. Arnold officiated in the installation of the officers in their various offices.—C. C. Hamby was re-installed Master. The installation ceremonies were very impressive. At the close of the proceedings, a very interesting and instructive address was read by Dr. E. R. Armistead, followed by an extemporaneous speech by Hon. W. E. Atkinson, delivered in his usual eloquent and happy style. Quite a large crowd of ladies and gentlemen were present on the occasion.

The picnic near Hickory Grove, last Saturday was a grand success. Early in the morning the people from the immediate neighborhood began to gather at a place call Loomis' old mill stand, and were soon joined by citizens from Prescott and Emmet. The forenoon was taken up in a Sunday school review, after which it was announced that all were respectfully invited to dinner. This part of the program was excellent, the long tables were actually filled to overflowing with good things. In the evening Rev. R. M. Traylor made an appropriate talk to the good people and was followed by Mr. Edward Hamm who made a short speech. The people of this community are all wide-a-wake farmers, and look to each other's interest. They treated the visitors with a hospitality that is bound to win.

Henry Jones, a negro, was lynched by a mob at Woodland Mills, Tenn., a few nights ago. Jones had murdered a white man in cold blood a few nights before.

Natural gas has been struck in abundant quantities in the Sequatchie Valley, twenty-two miles west of Chattanooga, Tenn.

Miss Tilla Coleman was burned to death at Birmingham, Ala., a few days since. While lighting a fire with kerosene her clothing ignited and she rushed from the house wrapped in flames and rolled down a flight of stairs into the midst of a group of women, setting fire to half a dozen of them. The house was burned down.

County Judge J. Tartar, of Somerset, Ky., was drowned in Pitman creek a few evenings since while attempting to cross it in his buggy. The stream was swollen by heavy rains. Congressman Frank Finley was in the buggy with him at the time, but jumped out and swam ashore. He made an effort to save his friend, but was unsuccessful. The horse and buggy were recovered. Judge Tartar leaves a widow and seven children.

Mrs. Jane Duke died at Hartford, Ky., a few days since in the ninety-seventh year of her age. She enjoyed the distinction of being the first white child born in Ohio County, a territory which at the time of her birth included more than one-third of Western Kentucky. She was in many respects a remarkable woman, and maintained her activity in a great degree, and her eyesight and memory up to the time of her death.

Harry Smart was sentenced in Louisville, Ky., a few days since, to imprisonment for life for killing Meisner Green and Belle Ward four months ago.

The jail at Greensburg, La., was burned a few nights ago. There was only one prisoner in the building, a young negro charged with horse-stealing; he was cremated.

I. S. Albritton, a "picked" juror in an Atlanta (Ga.) murder trial, has been sentenced to jail for twenty days and to pay a fine of $200.

At North Birmingham, Ala., a few nights ago, Henry Brown, colored, shot and killed D. Johnson, white. The shooting was the result of a quarrel about some trivial matter. Brown escaped.

The report of the keeper of the Georgia penitentiary shows that during the last two years the proportion of female convicts in Georgia has increased more than twenty per cent.

Hon. John P. Campbell, an able lawyer and ex-member of Congress, died suddenly at his home in Hopkinsville, Ky., recently, in the sixty-ninth year of his age. He was at one time a member of the Missouri Legislature.

John Corbitt died recently at Nashville, Tenn., from the effects of an overdose of laudanum, taken with suicidal intent. The cause of the deed is not known, but it is supposed that he was suffering from mental aberration.

Andrew Johnson, a cripple, living near Red Hill, Ky., while digging in the ground, recently, unearthed a copper kettle filled with gold and silver coins. The kettle was inscribed "October, 1788." The treasure amounted to over $2,000.

Fire at Lynchburg, Va., a few days ago, destroyed Moorman's tobacco warehouse; the Dental chewing-gum factory; Hefernan's sash, blind and door establishment, and Ainslie & Bro's carriage works, causing a loss of over $50,000; insurance; $21,000.

Governor Seay of Alabama has removed the civil and political disabilities of John R. Taukersley, of Crenshaw County, convicted of murder in 1878, and sentenced to the penitentiary for ten years. He was discharged from prison last year and the Governor, in response to strong petitions, restored him to the rights and privileges of citizenship.

Joe Williams, Hardy Pope, Hardy Lewis and Jack Bailey escaped from the jail at Kingston, Tenn., a few days ago. When the sheriff and jailer opened the door the quartet pounced on them and after securing the sheriff's pistol made a break for liberty. After a lively chase, in which a large number of citizens joined, the jail birds were all recaptured.

At Fayetteville, Tenn., a few nights ago, Yerb McElroy, about eighteen years old, clerking in L. Garneau's bakery, became involved in a quarrel with ex-Policeman W. H. McCown, about the way some oysters were served. McElroy stabbed McCown in the throat, cutting an artery. McCown bled profusely, blood running from his eyes, ears and nose. He became very weak and was carried home, where he died the next morning.

Jesse Brundage, a twelve-year-old son of Mr. H. Brundage, of Leon, Ala., was accidentally killed a few days ago, at the steam gin of John Merrill. The boy stepped over a revolving shaft, which caught and twisted his clothing and whirled him over and over until his body was battered and bruised almost beyond recognition. He was dead when discovered. He was the son of mute parents, and a bright boy.

At Huntsville, Ga., a few nights ago, William Harrison, in an inexplicable fit of jealousy, shot his little niece without warning while sitting by the fireside. He then fired at his sister, wounding her in the hip. She will probably recover. Harrison fled, but returned, admitted his crime, and said he had attempted suicide by jumping into a well. Later he denied all knowledge of the crime. Harrison said he had been drinking heavily.

A remarkable scene was witnessed in Atlanta, Ga., a few nights ago. Ten thousand indignant citizens congregated in front of the court-house to testify their disgust for a jury which acquitted George Eddleman, a murderer, against whom was most conclusive evidence. He killed Thomas Gresham in a cruel and unprovoked manner, and every body expected his conviction. The jurors were burnt in effigy. Many of the best citizens were in the crowd. There was great excitement, but no disturbance occurred. Eddleman has left Atlanta. If he returns he will certainly be lynched.

Yellow fever will not down.

A stranger named Charles Emory was killed by a train on the East Tennessee road, near the East corporation line of Chattanooga, Tenn., a few nights ago. He was standing in the middle of the track when the train approached him and refused to heed the signal of the engineer.

Robert Echelberger, a young man from St. Louis, while coupling cars in the yards of the New Orleans & Northeastern railway, at Meridian, Miss., a few days ago, caught his left foot under the wheel of a loaded flat car. Six wheels passed over and his leg was fearfully mangled. He died from his injuries.

Elmon Slider, seven years old, is in jail at Louisville, Ky., for burglary.

Miss Mosse McGann, of Canada, a teacher of articulation in the Mississippi Institute for the Deaf and Dumb, died at Jackson, Miss., recently, after a lingering illness. Miss McGann's name as a successful teacher was known in every institution for the deaf and dumb in the United States and Canada.

A LYNCHING IN GEORGIA
GOV. GORDON'S THIRD RESPITE LEADS TO MOB LAW.
Night to Find Himself Surrounded by Masked Men With Guns—The Negro Swung From the Court-House Banister.

Rome, Ga., May 1.—Henry Pope, the negro who was convicted of assault with attempt to commit rape, at the last term of court in Chattooga county, was taken from the jail at Summerville last night by an armed mob and hanged. Gov. Gordon had issued a respite for sixty days and given it to the Principal Keeper of the Penitentiary, Col. J. R. Towers. He came to Rome yesterday and gave it to Sheriff J. C. Moore, of Floyd county, with instructions from the Governor to proceed to Summerville and bring the prisoner to Rome, for the purpose of having him taken to the Fulton county jail in Atlanta. Sheriff J. C. Moore, with an assistant, Charles Randall, left at 2 o'clock this afternoon, and arrived at Summerville at 8:30 o'clock to-night. The night was rainy and very dark. On their arrival they proceeded to Judge Maddox's house. After a consultation with the Judge, he said he was satisfied that they could not take him away that night, and he said he would meet them at sunrise in the morning at the jail with two guards, and that he would himself accompany them across the mountain. The Judge then sent for Sheriff Worsham, of Chattooga county. Upon his arrival he also advised waiting until morning before taking any action.

THE LYNCHING.

Sheriff Moore and his assistant then went to the hotel and retired at 11 o'clock, and about 2 o'clock Sheriff Worsham came and awoke them, stating that he had been awakened by a crowd and found the door of his room, which is in the jail, fastened and guarded by about fifteen armed men. He stated that a mob of about fifty masked men went to the jail and demanded the keys and the rope that was purchased at Rome a few days ago. They then secured Pope, and, putting the rope around his neck and putting out the lights, led him to the court house, about 150 yards distant, and hung him from the banisters at the top of the stairs. The Sheriff stated that crowds of armed men stood at the corners of each street. Judge Maddox went to the court house, and sent for a doctor. They cut the rope and took the body of Pope down and carried it into the court house. A doctor arrived and found life extinct. The news of the respite published yesterday was carried to Summerville by parties who arrived about two hours before the Sheriff.

HAD BEEN CONVICTED TWICE.

Henry Pope had been twice convicted of an assault upon Miss Minnie Kendrick, in Chattooga county, on February 3, 1887, and was respited by Gov. Gordon Saturday night upon the affldavits of five repectable men that Pope was fifty miles from the scene of the crime on the day it was committed. It was known to Gov. Gordon that there was intense feeling against Pope in Chattooga County and he endeavored to keep the respite secret until Col. Towers would have had time to get to Summerville and bring the prisoner out of the County. Summerville is in the country, 25 miles from Rome, but there is a telephone line from Rome to Tryon factory. The latter place is only 5 miles from Summerville and people are passing from one place to the other often. It is very probable that in this way the news of the respite reached Summerville early in the afternoon.

HOW HE WAS SWUNG.

Sheriff Moore says it looks as though the rope was put on Pope's neck and he was then thrown off the balcony. His neck was not broken. The Sheriff was sleeping in the jail and was awakened by a demand for his keys, backed by about fifteen shotguns. There was nothing for him to do but to give them up. The crowd then took a rope and hung Pope. Miss Minnie Kendricks was going through some woods between her home and the home of a neighbor in Chattooga county Thursday, Feb. 3, 1887. In the woods she met a negro who assaulted her. When she escaped from him she gave an alarm, and the country was scoured for miles around. Several negroes were arrested and brought to Miss Kendrick, who promptly declared as each one was brought that he was not the man.

HIS CAPTURE.

On May 4, 1887, Henry Pope was arrested in Cherokee county, Alabama, and was brought to Summerville May 7. The popular indignation was so great against him that a special guard was organized for the prisoner's protection. A special term was called and held May 9, 1887, and Henry Pope was convicted and sentenced to be hanged July 1. In the court room, as in the jail, the prisoner was guarded by armed men to protect him from the people, who were infuriated against him because of the crime, which they thought he had committed. After the announcement of the verdict the Judge advised the counsel for the defendant not to make a motion for a new trial, because he was apprehensive that in that event a mob would attempt to hang Pope, and good men would be killed in an effort to defend him. The Governor, on June 28, issued an order respiting Pope till Sept. 2, 1887. On Aug. 29 a further respite was granted until Nov. 4. Pending his second respite Judge Maddox granted a new trial on an extraordinary motion. The trial took place during the first week in March, 1888. Pope was again convicted and sentenced to be hanged on May 2 (to-morrow). Gov. Gordon was again petitioned to respite Pope, and the petition was accompanied by such strong evidence to prove an alibi that a respite was granted for sixty days.

INNOCENT MAN HANGED.
Masked Georgia Lynchers Commit a Gross Outrage on Justice.
Outrage on Justice.

ATLANTA, GA., May2.—In Georgia the simple word of a sixteen-year old girl convicts a man of attempting an outrage, against the sworn testimony of numbers of Alabama's best citizens, who swear to have seen the man in Alabama on the day the crime was committed. Henry Pope, colored, was lynched by a mob of fifty masked men at Summerville, in Chattooga county, this morning, at half-past two o'clock. Pope was lynched for a crime of which there is every reason to believe him innocent. In February,1887, Miss Minnie Kendrick, a sixteen-year old girl, while going through some woods between her home and the house of a neighbor in Chattooga county, was assaulted by a colored man. Upon escaping

SHE GAVE THE ALARM.

The woods were scoured and several persons were arrested, but upon being brought face to face with each man Miss Kendrick promptly exonorated him and the search continued.

In May of the same year Henry Pope was arrested in Cherokee county, Alabama, fifty miles from the scene of the outrage. He was placed in company with twenty others, and Miss Kendrick was then asked to see if the man who assaulted her was there. She immediately singled out Henry Pope and said: "He is the man who did the deed. I remember him by his wicked and cruel eyes." Upon this testimony alone Pope was convicted and sentenced to be hanged. Against the testimony of this weak girl were the affidavits of nine men who swore that they were residents of Cherokee county, Alabama, and that Pope was at work there on the day the crime was committed. Among these were his employer, who swore that he worked for him on that day, a merchant who sold him goods on the day of the crime and numerous citizens who saw him, and who swore that he could not have got to Chattooga county if he had tried.

THE AFFIDAVITS OF THESE MEN,
Together with certificates from every county official in Cherokee county as to the high character and disinterestedness of the men who made the affidavits, were sent to Governor Gordon, who respited the prisoner three times, until further proof of his innocence could be had.

He was to be hanged to-day, but was again respited at the earnest request of every leading man in Cherokee county. Fearing trouble when the respite was known, Governor Gordon determined to move the prisoner from Chattooga county to Atlanta, Ga., and sent the Superintendent of the Penitentiary for him. He was to have been removed today. Last night fifty masked men, carrying shotguns, forced the janitor to give up the keys of the jail, secured the prisoner and hung him from the Court House banisters in Summerville, the county seat of Chattooga county. The deed is greatly deplored all over the State, as it is feared a great mistake has been made. The prisoner declared his innocence to the last.

A DOUBLE-FACED FRAUD.
Mr. Roger Q. Mills, of Texas, who is now making free-trade speeches in Indiana, has two tones to his voice. When he poses as the leader of Democracy and mouth-piece of the administration he is a rampant free-trader, but when he wants to obtain votes under false pretenses he is a mild protectionist. Thus in a speech in the House of Representatives he said:

"Wealth, prosperity and power will bless the land that is dedicated to free men, free labor and free trade."

To a delegation of Philadelphia wool-merchants he said:

"The more confusion the tariff works to business the better I like it, because it will the sooner be done away with. I desire free trade, and I will not help to perfect any law that stands in the way of free trade."

A still later expression is in an article in Belford's Magazine for August, on the "Real Issue," in which he says:

"We have lived to be thankful that that relation [of slavery] was wiped out, how much soever we may lament the gallant dead and the wasted treasure. And the time will come when all the people will rejoice to see this business relation [of protection] a darker evil than that of slavery—eliminated from the land. It is a darker evil; for while the Southern system of unrequited toil enslaved the blacks, this system is reducing white labor to slavery, and we revenue-reformers, or free-traders, if we may so be called, are making our fight for our own race, whose misery keeps pace with our prosperity."

Here the Texas statesman goes so far as to denounce protection as a darker evil than slavery. As he never opposed slavery and does oppose protection, we cannot doubt his sincerity.

But in the speech he is making in this State Mr. Mills says:

"Let us see what sort of a bill we have presented. It is very moderate. We have reduced the average taxation from $47.10 on $100 to $42.50 on $100; a little less than $5 on $100 on imported goods. Is that free trade? If it is, I would like to know what they mean by protection."

He dares not stand up before an Indiana audience and advocate free trade by name as he does in fact. He dares not say, as he did to the Philadelphia merchants, that he desires free trade, and will not help to perfect any law that stands in the way of it. He dares not denounce protection as "a darker evil than slavery," though his record shows he thinks it so. Instead of that he adopts the contemptible, cowardly 5 per cent. lie, and tells his Indiana audiences that his bill reduces the "protection robbery" only 5 cents on the dollar. Mr. Mills, of Texas, is a bigger fraud than his bill.

THE Democrats are trying to make capital out of the alleged fact that General Harrison was paid $1,000 for about a week's service in an important law case. Suppose that were true, which it isn't, the services rendered were worth the money, and the people of the

United States are hunting a man worth a thousand dollars a week. That is the salary of President of the United States, and they want a man with brains and experience enough to be worth the amount, instead of further wasting it on one who could not make fifty dollars a week anywhere if he was thrown on his own resources.

A TEMPEST IN A TEA-POT.

The fuss kicked up over two incidents of the political demonstration last Saturday night is entirely unworthy all engaged in making and fomenting it. One incident was the reported assault upon a member of the Frances Cleveland Club by a colored man, which is magnified into a most dastard thing, and there were threats of lynching made by the excited Democratic hoodlums in the locality. The evidence shows that one of the marching women dropped her handkerchief, which a colored boy, sixteen years of age, attempted to pick up with a broken cane he held in his hands. The girl slapped him in the face, and the boy retaliated by hitting her with the shortened cane. That was all there was of it, and for the assault the boy was fined $5 and costs yesterday. The fine was utterly disproportionate to the offense, and should not have been imposed.

The other incident is that of the police interference with some of the citizens, and afterward with some of the Chicago visitors near the Denison House. The evidence is conclusive that it was unnecessary impertinence on the part of one or two Democratic patrolmen, supplemented by indiscreet zeal on the part of Captain Colbert, who has several times previously shown himself unfit for the responsibilities of his place. It would have been a very proper thing if the overofficious policemen had been thrown into the middle of the street.

Such incidents must be expected in a political campaign. The duty of the police is to preserve the peace, not to threaten it by unnecessary interference, and engaging in wrangles with good-natured lookers-on. A Republican has a perfect right to cheer for Harrison and Morton, though there be ten thousand Democrats on parade instead of five, and if a cheer for Harrison is so offensive as to make it likely that a Democratic parade will be thrown into spasms and broken up, the delicate creatures will have to become hardened to such experiences. The policeman who cannot tell a good-natured and perfectly proper expression by a man or a crowd from a deliberate and malignant attempt to breed trouble, as when Grandfather Jones's "reform" postoffice bummers stand on the curb and yell insulting epithets at Republican paraders, should be promptly relieved.

There is a tempest in a teapot. The sooner it is over the more creditable to all parties. And in the meantime, conceding that the action of one or more of the Chicago visitors may have passed the bounds of prudence, the less the public hears from Chairman Jewett about "holding General Harrison responsible" for alleged outrages to tender Democratic susceptibilities the better for his reputation. Such talk is the talk of a tuppenny "ward worker," not of a man worthy to be the campaign leader of a great party.

nesses the defense asked for a continuance of the case, and by agreement it went over until a week from next Monday.

Walved Examination.

George Turnage, arrested for the killing of William McGill, waived examination before the Mayor, yesterday morning, and was committed to jail to await the action of the grand jury. He says he desires a speedy trial. His defense will be that he had no idea of seriously injuring the man when he struck him, and that the fracture of the skull, resulting in death, came from the fall on the pavement.

Suit for Damages.

The suit of Mary A. Wise against the Citizens' Street-railway Company for damages on account of personal injuries is on trial before a jury in Judge Walker's room. While attempting to alight from a street car on Washington street, several months ago, Mrs. Wise's clothing caught on the rear step, and she was dragged some distance.

Declared Insane.

Mrs. Georgia Class, living at No. 26½ Massachusetts avenue, was declared insane yesterday by a commission composed of Drs. King and White, and Justices Smock and Judkins. Her insanity, the physicians say, has resulted from a nervous disease with which she has been affected for several years.

Both Want the Child. The divorce suit of Mamie Ellis against Horace E. Ellis, is attracting some attention in Judge Walker's court on account of a contest for custody of their child. The case proper has not yet come to trial, but upon an affidavit filed by the wife making serious charges against Mr. Ellis, Judge Walker yesterday gave the child into the custody of its maternal grandmother. Mr. Ellis at once filed an affidavit charging that the woman into whose custody the child had been given was unfit to care for it, and asking that it be returned to him. The court will pass upon the affidavit this morning, and if he does not grant the request habeas corpus proceedings will likely be brought. A Bit of Democratic Malice.
Samuel M. Booker, the colored youth fined by Mayor Denny, Monday morning, for striking a young lady in the Democratic procession, Saturday night, was arrested again yesterday through Democratic malice, and arraigned before 'Squire Walpole, on the charge of striking Louisa Eckert the same night. When Miss Eckert was brought into court she testified that Booker was not the boy who struck her, and he was released. The colored men of the city are very indignant over the way a few Democrats have attempted to make trouble for young Booker, against whom nothing was ever before charged.

John Oliver's Sentence.

John Oliver pleaded guilty before Judge Irvin yesterday to obtaining money under false pretenses and was sentenced to one year's imprisonment in the penitentiary. Oliver's crime was what is vulgarity known as the "dead wife racket." He was employed by Haugh, Ketcham & Co., and desiring to raise money on which he could get out of the city had a confederate telephone to the works that his wife was dead. He then asked his fellow-workmen for a contribution with which to pay funeral expenses, and received a considerable sum. His wife had not even been sick.

A Promise of Good Behavior.

Lula Fred, charged with petty thieving, was released yesterday by Judge Irvin on her promising to mend her ways. She pleaded guilty to the charge, but furnished evidence that she had always been trustworthy until she got into this difficulty.

On a Change of Venue.

The case against A. D. Loy, of Hendricks county, charged with assault and battery with intent to kill, was called in the criminal cours here, yesterday, on a change of venue.

SMUGGLED FROM SPARTANBURG.
A Negro Prisoner who Barely Escaped Lynching.
COLUMBIA, S. C., July 31.—Deputy Sheriff Gentry, of Spartanburg, arrived here this morning with Ira Waters for safe keeping. The deputy and prisoner had been on the road since yesterday morning. Waters was charged with attempting a criminal assault on a white woman in upper Spartanburg. He was placed in jail last Wednesday. Yesterday morning a party of white men came to Spartanburg for the purpose of lynching him. As soon as their purpose became known the deputy smuggled Waters out of the jail and took to the woods with him. They caught the train for Greenwood, where there being no jail, the negro was chained in a room all night. They arrived here this evening much used up. Waters is handcuffed and the key is lost.

Secretary Marshall issued a commission Thursday to the Royal bag manufacturing company of Charleston. The incorporators are: George A. Wagener, James M. Seignious, B. F. McCabe, William M. Bird and E. C. Williams, Jr., all of Charleston. The purpose of the company is to manufacture all kinds of bags, brooms and woodenware. The capital stock will be $30,000.

The alligators in the lower portion of South Carolina attain an immense size, and frequently catch dogs and hogs, and sometimes horses and cattle, but they seldom attack a man. A party of boys were bathing in the river near Georgetown Tuesday, only a short distance from shore, when an alligator, about twelve feet long, appeared in the midst of the bathers, and, seizing a 12-year old boy, disappeared with its prey. Nothing has since been seen of the boy, so at least says a correspondent of the New York Sun.

The stockholders of the Aiken county loan and savings bank of Aiken met Wednesday for permanent organization; $40,000 out of $50,000 capital stock was represented in person and by proxy. The following were elected directors of the bank: W. W. Woolsey, W. M. Hutson, J. W. Ashhurst, H. H. Hall, H. F. Warneke, H. B. Burckhalter, Henry Hahn, C. H. Phinizy of Augusta, Ga, and George W. Williams, Jr., of Charleston. Upon the adjournment of the stockholders' meeting the board of directors met and elected the following officers: W. W. Woolsey, president; W. M. Hutson, vice president; J. W. Ashhurst, cashier. The bank will open its doors for business on Sept. 1.

Fred Sadler, son of David Sadler of Dark Corner township, in Anderson county, and Willie Hodges, two cousins, about 16 years old, were playing with a pistol, the property of Willie. Fred extracted the load from the pistol, as he thought, and then told Willie there was his pistol; that he had taken the cartridges out of it with his knife. He then raised it and said: "Now I've got the advantage of you." The reply was: "I will shoot you for it," and both, in the most playful spirit, turned on each other. Fred had the knife drawn and Willie took the supposed unloaded pistol, cocked it and snapped at Fred. To his surprise it fired, the ball taking effect in Fred's side. The unfortunate boy exclaimed "I'm shot," and fell dead.

At Orangeburg Wednesday, Chief of Police W. H. Perryclear, on a telegram from the sheriff of Augusta, Richmond county, to Sheriff Salley, arrested Columbus L. Ward, charged in Augusta with assault and battery with intent to kill. Ward is originally from Greenville, S. C., and it is said by those who know him that he is a desperate character. He is about 6 feet tall, and weighs about 180 pounds. Chief Perryclear says he has reason to believe that this Ward is the same man who escaped from the Chattahoochee brick company of Atlanta in January last, taking with him a wagon and a pair of mules and a double-barrelled gun. Ward is being held, awaiting a requisition on the governor for him.

An important meeting of the board of directors of the Carolina, Knoxville and Western Railway company was held at Greenville Tuesday, the special object being to receive the first completed section of the new road, extending five miles from where the line connects with the Greenville and Laurens road in the city. On the report of Chief Engineer Stone this section was accepted by the executive committee of the directors, and the American Trust company of New York was ordered to pay to the Georgia Construction company from funds held in trust for the railroad company the amount due by contract for building the first five miles, being $40,000 per mile, one-half in stock and one-half in first mortgage bonds.

Deputy Sheriff J. J. Gentry of Spartanburg arrived at Columbia Tuesday with a negro prisoner named Ira Waters, brought for safe keeping. There about a week ago Waters was arrested upon the charge of attempting a criminal assault on a white woman and was taken to Spartanburg and lodged in jail. The scene of the alleged crime was sixteen miles north of Spartanburg. It was claimed that Waters would have accomplished his purpose, but was prevented by the approach of some white men. Nothing further was thought of the matter by Sheriff Gentry of Spartanburg, until two days ago when it was reported to him that threats of lynching had been made, and that a party of white men from the section of the county where the crime was believed to have been committed were going to Spartanburg to take the prisoner from the jail. Early Monday morning a party of men from that section came into Spartanburg, and it was understood they were only awaiting reinforcements before attacking the jail. Sheriff Gentry immediately instructed his son, J. J. Gentry, to take the prisoner from the jail, leave the city as secretly as possible and bring him to Columbia. The deputy sheriff took Waters out of the rear entrance of the jail and proceeded out of the town. He footed it through the country about fifteen miles, and finally boarded a train on the Laurens road.

NO LONGER A MYSTERY.
gulch, in the coast range mountains, near San Felipe, discovered a grave containing the bones of a woman and many gold and silver trinkets.

This discovery has solved a mystery that for a long time has puzzled the inhabitants of the San Joaquin valley, as there is but little doubt that the remains were those of Zarifa Martinique, the daughter of Jose Martinique, who, fifteen years ago, was sheriff of Fresno county. In a small iron chest found buried by the side of the skeleton were several Spanish coins and a faded photograph which bore the woman's name.

The grave was discovered at the foot of a tall redwood tree at the head of the gulch, and was surrounded by bowlers that had rolled down from the mountains above. In the trunk of the redwood were the initials Z. M. and J. R., cut deeply, and as it seemed, with a sharp knife. The remains were taken to San Felipe and buried in a plat in the cemetery, where sleep her father, mother and two brothers.

There is a romance connected with the life of Zarifa Martinique that the pioneer settler of the San Joaquin valley never fails to relate to the visitor. As the story goes, she was a beautiful girl, with the grace of an American mother and the heat of Spanish ancestors in her disposition. No man in the San Joaquin valley could hold the bit in a horse's mouth with steadier hand than could Zarifa, and she rode like a queen with or without a saddle. She could shoot with the accuracy of a practiced marksman, and possessed a spirit as fearless as a lion. She was a perfect type of the wild western girl, but the inhabitants of San Felipe, among whom she had been born and reared, loved the harum-scarum girl, for there was always a bright smile on her pretty face,
and in her bosom beat a heart as tender
and sympathetic as that of a child.

At the age of 18 years Zarifa was loved
and courted by Octave Morez, a young
Spanish rancher in the valley who had accumulated a considerable fortune, and her father was anxious that his only daughter should become the wife of Octave, but Zarifa, when the subject was broached to her, angered her father and astonished her suitor by declaring that her heart had long ago been given to Jack Raymond, and she should never marry if she could not be his wife. Jack Raymond, upon whom the sheriff's daughter had bestowed her affection, was a handsome fellow, shiftless and daring, who divided his time between the gaming table and prospecting for gold among the hills. In the latter pursuit he was generally successful', in the former he was always unfortunate, so that he managed with but little trouble to keep his accounts balanced. No one accused Jack of being bad at heart, but he was looked upon as a fellow absolutely worthless to himself and everybody else. Jack and Zarifa had met, and between the handsome spendthrift and the beautiful girl had sprung up a mutual affection that was nursed until it grew to mad infatuation.

When Zarifa's father learned the trend of his daughter's love, he instituted a series of persecutions against Jack, in the hope of driving him from the country. He was frequently thrown into jail on petty charges, and as often set free after paying a heavy fine, for the courts were with the sheriff and the community was prejudiced against Jack, so that it was a hard matter for him to establish his innocence of any charge brought against him. But he had friends in his own class who stood faithfully by him.

These persecutions on the part of her father seemed only to strengthen the love of Zarifa for Jack, and her dislike for Morez grew into open hatred, which exasperated the young rancher beyond control, and he swore vengeance on Raymond, openly vowing to shoot him on sight if he ever again showed public recognition of Zarifa. One day, while Jack was seated by a table in a saloon conversing with friends, Morez came in much the worse for drink, and recognizing his rival uttered an oath, and, drawing his revolver, opened fire on him. Jack drew his own pistol and with unerring aim sent a bullet through his rival's heart. Knowing his popularity in that community, Jack fled the town, taking refuge in the mountains, and though diligent search was made for him under the direction of the sheriff, the hiding place of the refugees could not be found.

Zarifa never lost track of her lover. In Sulphur Gulch, under the old redwood where her remains were found, the two had met for months, and this trysting place had always been kept a secret between them. Here the two continued to meet after Jack was a fugitive from justice. Zarifa owned a horse, a fiery black animal, the gift of her father, and on this horse she was in the habit of taking daily rides through the valley. So persistently did she continue this custom after Jack's disappearance, and so long did she remain absent each day, the suspicions of her father were aroused, and through carefully following her he one day discovered the tryst, and a week later, with a posse of citizens, managed to capture Jack, who was taken back in triumph to San Felipe and lodged in prison.

Zarifa was inconsolable, for she knew that her father would never be satisfied until Jack was dead, and she knew he had sufficient influence in that community to carry out any plan he might form. She could see no escape for her lover. The jail in which he was imprisoned was carefully guarded and she could lend him no assistance, but she did not despair. She watched her father with the cunning of a cat.

The sheriff thirsted for Jack's blood, although he knew he had killed Morez in self defense, for he had ruined his prospects for becoming father-in-law to the richest rancher in the San Joaquin valley. His Spanish blood was up to white heat, and he spent day and night in the saloons of San Felipe haranguing against Jack Raymond and urging the citizens to see that in his case the ends of justice were not cheated. The words of the sheriff were effectual, for he was a man of influence and his utterances were not to be considered lightly. One night a mob with their brains aflame with whisky and the fiery speech of the sheriff set out with a rope for the jail, bent on lynching Raymond. The sheriff headed the mob, and this gave them courage. The jail was reached, and the jailer, seeing the determination of his visitors and recognizing in their leader the sheriff of the county,

"String 'im up, then, boys," yelled the sheriff, "let's git rid of 'im as soon as we can; it's too d—d wet and cold to be foolin' around here."

The noose was quickly adjusted about Jack's neck, around him was a living circle and at the other end of the rope stood a dozen sturdy men, anxiously waiting for the sheriff to give the signal to settle back on it. He was but a single step from eternity. The half dozen lanterns fluttered and gasped in the rain and surrounded the victim with a weird, ghastly halo. "When I count three, boys," said the sheriff, "pull back on 'im," and immediately he cried "one," and then "two," his voice had just begun to swell into the "three," and the men at the end of the rope with tightening muscles had just begun to brace themselves for a "long pull and a strong pull," when there was the clatter of galloping feet and the rush of a black lady through the lines into the middle of the circle. Before the half paralyzed mob could recover its senses the sheriff's daughter had cut the ropes that encircled her lover's neck and bound his hands. She shouted to him to mount the horse in front of her. He was up in an instant, and before the men sent sprawling in the mud by the horse had recovered their senses Jack and the sheriff's daughter were rattling away through the darkness with the speed of the wind toward the mountains. Several shots were sent into the darkness after them, but they went wide of the mark.

From that night to the day her remains were discovered Zarifa Martinique was never seen by the inhabitants of the San Joaquin valley, nor could the retreat of her lover, who became a notorious outlaw, be discovered. Three fingered Jack, as Raymond came to be known in after years, became the terror of the San Joaquin valley, and no less than seven of the men who had attempted to lynch him were sent to their graves by bullets from his rifle. Eight years ago he was captured in a desperate saloon fight in Red Cliff and hanged for his crimes. Before his execution he sent for Jose Martinique, and in an interview told him that his daughter had lived with him five years, then died, and that he had buried her remains in the mountains near his retreat, where nobody could find and disturb them. On the gallows he cursed Martinique roundly, and charged him with being the cause of his turning his hand against the law and the people. Jose Martinique became demented and roamed among the mountains, continually searching for the grave of his child. His body was found one morning at the bottom of Sulphur Gulch, where he had died of exposure and exhaustion.—Chicago Herald.

AN ALABAMA MOB RIDDLES WITH BULLETS A NEGRO
WHO HAD COMMITTED NO CRIME.
CHICAGO. March 20.—A dispatch from Birmine-
CHICAGO, March 20.—A dispatch from Birmingham, Ala., says: Jeff Curry, a negro, who worked in the Blue Creek mines, a few miles from this city, and who was under arrest, was taken from the officers who had him, in charge Sunday night and shot by a mob of unknown men, his body being completely riddled with bullets. Curry had a dispute with a miner named Powell, but no blows were exchanged. Shortly afterward Powell caused the negro's arrest, charging him with carrying concealed weapons. Shortly after dark two officers started with him for this city, where they were to place him in jail. When they came to a deserted spot in the road they were suddenly attacked by the mob, who took their prisoner from them, and, leading him a short distance away, commenced diving. Curry dropped dead instantly, and his murderers made their escape.

French Canadians Offended.

ONTREAL, March 20.—At a meeting of persons opposed to the action of the French vice-consul here flying his flag at half-mast in respect to the memory of the dead emperor of Germany, it was resolved to protest against his action, and a committee was appointed to secure signatures in support of the protest.

Opening a New Railway in Mexico.

CITY OF MEXICO, March 20.—The railway branch extending from Marquez, on the Central Trunk Line, to Hacienda Astillera, was opened Sunday. A large party, including Gen. Pacheco, minister of public works, went over the line in a special train. The road, which is about 38 kilometers long, was built by Carlos Eisenmann, in conjunction with a party of Berlin capitalists. A German syndicate has agents here looking out for land investments.

From Wall Street To Day.

NEW YORK, March 20. 11 a.m.—There was a moderate degree of animation in the stock market at the time, this morning, but the first sales were made at corporations from last evening's closing sale, which was 40 % or cent, the latter in Missouri Public and Louisianaville and Nashville. The activity, which was caused to a few leading stocks, among which Banc of Pacific, Reading, Missouri Pacific, Western Union, Lackawanna and St. Paul were conspicuous, was of short duration only, the market settling down to the usual dullness after the first quarter hour. An improving tendency was manifested at first and slight fractional gains were established, but the advantage was not maintained and most of the list retired to a shade below the opening figures, Missouri Pacific showing weakness, with a loss of 5 % per cent. There was no further movement in the market, and at 11 o'clock it was very dull and steady, generally at small fractions below the opening figures.

PECULIAR JUSTICE.
How a Negro Was Served by Alabama Officials.
How a Negro Was Served by Alabama Officials.

Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., March 19.—Yesterday morning, down near Bessimer, two white men named Powell, father and son, fell out with Jeff Curry, a negro cobbler, about a job he had done for one of them. and pistols were drawn on both sides, but not fired. Shortly afterward they had him arrested and taken before a magistrate, who ordered him brought to this city to jail, two white men being appointed to escort him. During the afternoon the negro's body was found with a handful of buckshot in it, his clothes being fairly riddled. An inquest was held before the same magistrate, but nothing was brought out as to who did the shooting. Several names are connected with it in the neighborhood though, and warrants have been sworn out for the parties. The guards' story is that a mob of disguised men took the negro from them and killed him, but inasmuch as one of them was seen in consultation with one of the Powelis just before setting out with the prisoner, it is suspected that they knew more about the personnel of the mob than they care to tell. The friends of the Powells, it is said: were overheard after the quarrel arranging with them a scheme to hide behind a rock on the road and shoot him.

CHICAGO, March 20.—A dispatch from Birmingham, Ala., says: Jeff Curry, a negro who worked in the Blue-Creek mines, a few miles from this city, and who was under arrest, was taken from the officers who had him in charge Sunday night and shot by a mob of unknown men, his body being completely riddled with bullets. Curry had a dispute with a miner named Powell, but no blows were exchanged. Shortly afterwards Powell caused the negro's arrest, charging him with carrying concealed weapons. Shortly after dark two officers started with him for this city, where they were to place him in jail. When they were at a deserted spot in the road they were suddenly attacked by a mob, who took the prisoner from them and leading him a short distance away commenced firing. Curry dropped dead instantly, and his murderers made their escape.

We share with the people of Jackson in their grief for Gen'l Wirt Adams' death, for we knew him well, and more than esteemed him. But we would not abate an iota of the remorseful culpability which that community feels for his tragic taking off. It has permitted and tolerated the growth and sway of journalism unrestrained by sense of responsibility or justice, contemning the duties as well as the decencies of the calling; and at last, by indulgence, reckless of the consequences which its abuses were sure to entail Once fixed in Jackson, this evil spirit seems to have emasculated and terrorized public sentiment; only to be aroused when brought to view the bloody and lifeless form of the most respected and loved of its populace, who in his three score and tenth year, is goaded into taking the streets to vindicate an unsullied name from continuous, unprovoked, vile and devilish abuse. Honor's very soul and embodiment, generous, considerate and courtly toward all men, lustred with a clean and heroic life; General Adams should have had a gentler end. That he had not, that he "was done to death by slanderous tongues," is an enduring reproach at the door of Jackson. Had the men of that city but been true to their manhood, had they unitedly pronounced disfavor upon this ribald journalism from whose envenomed shafts no citizen is safe, it could never have perpetuated itself. If Gen'l Adams was not secure against published scurrility, who is? What was there in this simple, kindly old gentleman to attract it? SANDY HILL UP IN ARMS.
A LITTLE GIRL ASSAULTED NEAR HER SCHOOL BY A BALL PLAYER.
A Crowd Attempts to Lynch the Culprit—The Mob Kept at Bay by a Policeman, Who Accidentally Shoots His Prisoner.

GLENS FALLS, Nov. 7.—The village of Sandy Hill, Washington county, was the scene of terrible excitement this afternoon. About 2 o'clock two little nine-year-old girls went to one of the outbuildings in the rear of the Union school. They were Helen Sherrill, daughter of Robert Sherrill, a manufacturer, and Nellie Lloyd, daughter of Daniel Lloyd. They were not on the threshold by John Glenn, a base ball player, formerly of Rochester, and he offered them candy. The children became frightened and started to run. The man caught hold of Helen Sherrill and assaulted her.

Fearing that the child's cries would bring help he tried to pitch her headlong into the vault. The child increased her struggles, and breaking from the man's clutches, dashed through the door across the yard and out of the gate. Her screams attracted a crowd, who started in pursuit of Glenn, following him up the street and across lots. Policeman Gilson Mason caught him after a long chase, and was taking his man to the station when by some means or other he broke away and sought refuge in the residence of M. G. Paris.

Policeman Morrison arrived opportunely, and entering the house, found Glenn hidden in the collar in a coal bin. He surrendered, was taken outside, put in a cart, and driven to the office of Police Justice Sullivan in the village.

There a crowd of several hundred men were gathered, armed with clubs, and arrangements were at once made for lynching the prisoner. As the cart rolled up to the sidewalk a rush was made for the man. Policeman Morrison drew his revolver, and ordered the crowd to stand back. Blows were aimed at the prisoner, many of them taking effect. The policeman fought his way to the foot of the staircase leading to the Justice's office, and, grasping Glenn with one hand, covered the angry crowd with his revolver.

Another rush was made, and in the scuffle that followed some one perked the policeman's arm so that the revolver was exploded, the ball entering Glenn's neck beneath the right jaw, and passing upward it lodged in the brain. Glenn fell to the ground, and for some minutes he was thought to be dead. After finding that the breath of life still remained in his body, he was removed to the house of his brother, where at last reports he was still alive.

Policeman Morrison was visited at his house this evening by many prominent citizens, who absolve him wholly from blame. If Glenn survives he will most assuredly be lynched. While he lived in Rochester he played ball with the old Alerts. It is said that he has been in State prison in the West for assaulting a woman, and about two years ago he assaulted his own niece. Last summer he fired one shot at a car driver while drunk, but did not hit him. He was arrested and fined. Had he not been shot to-day the mob would have succeeded in getting him away from the policeman and would have hanged him to the nearest lamp post. The child will recover.

LYNCHED A NEGRO. A Girl Accuses him of Assault and a Mob Takes him in Hand.
ASHEVILLE, July 15.—Yesterday about 1 o'clock a rumor reached here that an assault had been committed on Sallie Kate Parker, a white girl, 13 years of age, by a negro, in the northern suburbs of the city. The police were notified, and the country and town were searched closely for the guilty man. About 9 o'clock last night a negro named John Humphreys was arrested under strong suspicion. The girl had said that the negro had on a striped shirt and was barefooted. When arrested Humphreys had on a white shirt and shoes, but it was ascertained that he had taken off a striped shirt and put on a white one, and had put on shoes.

He was made to put on a striped shirt and take off the shoes, and was taken at once into the presence of the girl, who identified him immediately. The negro was then locked up in the city calaboose. Considerable excitement prevailed at the time, and whispers of lynching were heard. In order to avoid this, at 1 o'clock this morning the negro was put in the steel cage of the county jail.

About 3:15 A. M. a band of from twenty-five to forty masked men came to the jail, and before Deputy Sheriff James Worley, who had the jail in charge, was aware of it they were in the jail. He grabbed a gun and ran to the top of the steps and opened fire on the crowd, which was returned with a shower of bullets. The walls of the jail show that there was considerable firing, but no one was hurt as far as ascertained. Worley was overpowered, but would not give the combination to the cage lock.

The mob, being prepared with sledge hammers and crowbars, literally tore the cage to pieces, occupying fully an hour in doing it. They then took the negro out and hanged him to a tree about a quarter of a mile from the jail, within the city limits. As soon as released Sheriff Worley rang the fire bell, and soon headed a posse and tried to recover the prisoner, but was eluded by the mob.

The girl was waylaid on her way from town in a hollow in the woods. The negro crept up behind her and choked her. The girl's throat and face were torn. It is rumored that the negro made a full confession of his guilt before he was hanged.

Daylight.
Hutchison (Kan.). July 15th.—A cowboy walked into the Bank of La Junta at 1:20 o'clock yesterday afternoon and, covering Rufus Phillips with a revolver, ordered him to drop all the funds of the bank into a bag he placed on the counter. Centennial Celebration.

MARRIETTA (O.), July 15th.—The great Centennial celebration opened auspiciously to-day, favored with delightful weather. Great numbers were in attendance upon the opening, in Centennial Hall, at which Governor J. B. Foraker presided. The day was given up to religious observances.

The address of the day was by Right Rev. Bishop Gilmour, of Cleveland.

REMARKABLE ESCAPE.

An Aeronaut Falls 1,000 Feet Into a River and Escapes Injury.

CINCINNATI, July 15th.—At Coney Island, ten min-s above Cincinnati, to-night at 7 o'clock, Samuel Young made an ascent of 1,000 feet in a hot air balloon, and let go to make the descent by his parachute. The parachute, for 900 feet, did not open, and he went down into twenty-five feet of water in the river and sank to the bottom. When he came up he got tangled in the parachute, but was rescued by boatmen unhurt.

Potts' effort to Escape the Gallows.—WASHINGTON, N. C., July 13.—W. A. Potts, Jr., a young lawyer, who was to have been hanged here 10-day, attempted suicide last night by taking morphine. He was found by one of the prisoners about 6 o'clock this morning in an unconscious condition. The Sheriff was notified and medical aid promptly called in. On examination the doctors pronounced him in a dying condition. In a short time, however, he rallied and showed signs of recovery, and by 10 a.m. there was no doubt of his full and complete recovery. The Sheriff, recognizing his feeble condition, wired Gov. Scales for a respite until next week, to which an almost immediate reply was received granting the respite until the 17th. Potts had written a letter to the Sheriff thanking him for his kindness and stating that he had relieved him (the Sheriff) of a painful duty, also stating that the physicians were in no wise responsible for possession of the drug. Upon the reception of the respite from Gov. Scales the Sheriff placed a death-watch over the prisoner, with rigid instructions to allow him to see no one except the physicians. He made no response upon being told of his respite except to ask for how long it was granted. Potts states that he took between 25 and 30 grains of morphine, but the attending physicians say he could not have taken over 2 to 3.

[Potts again got hold of poison on Tuesday, took it, and died soon afterwards, cheating the gallows at last. Poor fellow.]

So we welcome the Union Labor Party, and trust that courage, wisdom and principle may characterize its movement. And it may be that in all this rise of parties the God of hosts has His Hand in it, and in the end the black man may receive that justice and protection he is entitled to under the constitution of the State and Nation.

Well, we have been startled again at the outrageous murder of a young man of color at Asheville a few weeks ago.

What a blot on the fair name and fame of that delightful section of the grand old State. We are often put to it to satisfy our mind as to the civilization and christianity of some people. The worst of the matter was the hanging of the wrong man, we were told.

This state of things cannot last forever. The colored man has suffered much at the hands of those who interpret the Bible for us and who wrote our theology, and who pretend to keep the commandments, one of which says: "thou shalt not kill."

We are a firm believer in Holy Writ and would direct the attention of these violators of law that it is written on the pages of the sacred volume, "He that shedeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be also shed."

See the truth of this in South Carolina where a white man was lynched by colored men.

With the continual increase in education of the race and such staunch friends as Dr. Haygood of Georgia, the day of lynching colored men in a wholesale manner will soon come to an end.

Ethiopia shall soon stretch her hands unto God, and His justice will not sleep forever.

Let colored men stop fawning and stand erect in the full statue of American manhood and go in to make for themselves character and have a proper regard for virtue, and in all their dealing with their fellow man let honesty be uppermost.

JUDGE LYNCH.

A Negro Desperado Hanged by a Mob at Hopkinsville, Kentucky.

HOPKINSVILLE, Ky., March 16.—John Skinner, a colored desperado, was lynechd here at 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon by 200 masked men armed with Winchesters. A rope and a cherry tree furnished all the needed apparatus. Skinner was in the county jail under indictment for shooting to kill Ballard Fourquean while the latter was returning home in his wagon one cold afternoon last December. He gave Skinner a seat in his vehicle.

When they had reached the place at which he was hung, Skinner got down on the pike and began cursing Mr. Fourquean, who, to avoid trouble, drove on, when the negro suddenly drew a revolver and fired, the bullet taking effect in Fourquean's bosom, inflicting a wound from which he cannot recover, though he may live for years.

As Skinner could only be sent to the penitentiary for five years under his indictment, Fourquean's friends concluded they would take the law in their own hands. There is also an indictment against him in the courts here for grand larceny. Skinner was an escaped convict sent up for house breaking many years ago, and was a thoroughly bad character.

When he asked who is there? The answer was "A true friend" and he believing the statement, opened the door, as it is nothing uncommon for him to have special calls by officers having in charge prisoners, at any hour of night. They then demanded to know where was "Skinner's" cell and being informed that he was locked in the middle cell of the upper story of the jail, proceeded up the steps and unlocking the two locks, six of the party rushed in the cell which was occupied by Bill Rawlins, Ed Vinson, Pig Green and "Skinner," all colored. The prisoners were lying down and were told "We have come for "Skinner," we want "Skinner." Instantly the other three prisoners pointing to where "Skinner" was lying down, said "That's him, that's him." "Skinner" raised up, and said "Gentlemen, this is me." They then told him they had come for him and wanted him. He asked them "please gentlemen, give me time to put my clothes on." They said "put 'em on, but be in a hurry, our time is short." They they called for ropes, and one of the party said "I have 'em in my pockets and drawing a cotton rope about thirty feet long and a leather hame string, proceeded to tie their prisoner's hands behind him with the leather strap and put the rope around his neck. He was then warned not to make any demonstration that would alarm the town, under the penalty of instant death. He replied: I'm not going to Holloo! Three of the party then took hold of the rope and the march to the two-horse wagon standing in the street just in front of the jail, was made. On arriving he was assisted into the wagon and driven off down south Webber street to Seventh, disappearing in the darkness. The most of the mob accompanied the wagon, only a dozen or so remaining around the jail for a half an hour when they left. Mr. Long was warned not to come out of his house for at least a half an hour after the crowd left, or he would be shot instantly.

Hopkinsville, Kentucky, Excited.
HOPKINSVILLE, Ky., March 19.—There was considerable excitement in town Friday morning, over a placard that adorned one of the stone pillars in front of the court house, supposed to have been posted there by a member of the mob that hung skinner. It was badly spelled, and evidently written in a disguised hand, and hinted at prominent citizens of this county as having taken a hand in the lynching. It justified the deed as a necessity, and warned all evil-doers to beware, or they will be summarily dealt with. It was signed "A Member of the Mob." and has created a good deal of stir among the petty thieves and lesser criminals of this community. Judge Little, of Owensboro, who is holding circuit court, has instructed the grand jury that it is their duty to thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the hanging of Skinner, and, if possible, find out all who were members of the mob, and indict such for murder.

Henry Skinner, a Negro Criminal, Found Dangling From a Limb. A Hopkinsville Mob Rids the Community of a Brute With No Redeeming Qualities.
Hopkinsville, Ky., March 14. (Special.)—John Henry Skinner, alias Cox, alias Reynolds, was taken from the county jail this morning by an orderly mob and hanged to a large cherry tree two miles west of Hopkinsville on the Cadiz road, where, or near by, this incarnate villain in pure wantonness shot down Mr. B. E. Forquean, an inoffensive citizen, on the night of November 18, 1887. A crowd, estimated variously at from one to two hundred persons, masked and

ARMED WITH WINCHESTER RIFLES, quietly marched up Main street and surrounded the court house. Ten men were stationed on the east side, and guarded the front entrance of the police headquarters, while about fifty turned down Sixth street, and into Webber. The jail was quickly surrounded. The leader, accompanied by about fifteen determined fellows, pushed through the gate that silently swung to behind them. The jailer, Geo. W. Long, was aroused, and came out into the hallway, unconscious of the fearful tragedy that was pending. When he asked "who is there?" a stern voice cried out, "a friend who wants to see you." The door was opened and

SIX MEN SEIZED THE JAILER and demanded of him the keys of the jail cell. The jailer answered that they couldn't have them. That his wife was absent with the keys in her possession. Mr. Long was then covered with six rifles, and admonished that if he made an outcry he would quickly enter into another world. One of the guards took the lamp left burning on the table near the door, and going into Mr. Long's private apartment found the keys on the wall. In the meantime the jailer demanded his little son, nine years old, to go up stairs and arouse his guests, A. B. Long, formerly jailer, R. B. Monk and Alex Walker. The little fellow delivered the message. One of the men sent the advice to the jailer not to act foolishly, but to turn over the keys. Mrs. Long rushed to the rear door to arouse the neighbors, but was suddenly confronted by a yard full of armed men. She then retraced her steps hurriedly, and going up stairs and raised the window facing Webber street. She was again balked in the effort to attract the neighbors or call for assistance, for as many as ten guns were pointed in her face. She came down and thought to protect her husband.

WANTED HIM BAD.

The spokesman remarked, "Uncle George, we don't want to hurt you, nor any of your excited family, but John Skinner we are going to have."

They made Mr. Long lead the way in his night garments and socks. He was forced to unlock the cell occupied by Shinner. Three of the men rushed in, while the others down stairs covered the jailer with guns cocked.

SKINNER WAS LYING DOWN.

He quickly took in the situation and coolly remarked: "Gentlemen, let me put on my clothes. My life has brought no one any good and I am thankful that my death, at least, may be a source of blessing to you murderers."

He was abruptly cut short with "be quick about it." His hands were tied behind him with a leather string, and a rope placed around his neck with the knot under the chin. Three of the mob held the rope and took up their silent, ominous march. They re-locked the cell door, and leading Mr. Long to his room remarked: "You stay in this house thirty minutes."

The jailer smilingly answered: "Gents, I think I'll do that," and then the mob proceeded up Webber street, and out Princeton until they came to the place where Fourqueean was shot. The rope was placed about a wild cherry tree, on a limb projecting across the street. The prisoner was made to stand flatfooted on a spring wagon. At the signal the vehicle was started, and the unfortunate man's soul was unceremoniously HURLED INTO ETERNITY.

He was strangled to death. The mob then dispersed leaving the ghastly figure swinging to the limb. The alarm was given by the jailer at 4 o'clock, when the news spread like wildfire, everybody seemed to rejoice that the country was rid of so desperate a character.

Skinner was a dangerous nuisance and a MENACE TO THE COMMUNITY.

He was sent to the penitentiary three years ago for grand larceny, and after serving two years he escaped while at work on the branch prison at Eddyville. He immediately went upon the highway, and with daring audacity perpetrated every crime known to the calendar of villainy, except murder. November 18, he waylayed B. F. Fourquean upon the highway and shot him down like a dog. Fortunately the victim recovered. Skinner robbed and outraged helpless people with impunity. He was finally captured at Clarksville by detectives. Subsequently he made a bold dash for liberty. His previous lawlessness and defiance of the law would make a thrilling chapter of crime. He was looked upon by every one as the most dangerous desperado that ever lived in this community, and his death, by violence, though lynching is condemned, was a just fate. There is great excitement among the colored population, but no sympathizers. They all rejoice that such a character has been disposed of.

Attempt to Blow Up a Lawyer's Dwelling House.
ERIE, PA., May 3.—An attempt was made to blow up the residence of Mr. Frank McClintock, a lawyer living in Union City. Gas-pipe bombs had been placed under Mr. McClintock's bedroom and one in another part of the house. The one at the front of the house exploded, and besides demolishing the house, wrecked the other buildings. Fortunately the family escaped with slight injuries. The outrage is believed to have been the result of recent prosecutors by McClintock of violations of the liquor license law, and also of several gangs of thieves and burglars. Frank Koehler was arrested last evening upon suspicion. He was a venomous hater of Mr. McClintock.

A Bomb Shattered His House.

UNION CITY, PA., AROUSED BY AN ATTEMPT TO KILL AN ANTI-LICENSE ATTORNEY.

An explosion that awoke the sleeping people within a radius of 3 miles and shattered window glass all over the town startled the inhabitants of Union City, Pa., at 2:30 Wednesday morning. An investigation showed that the residence of F. H. McClintock, in a thickly settled part of the town, had been partially destroyed by a dynamite bomb, which was placed against the front foundations, under the porch. A piece of 18-inch gas pipe, 16 inches long, plugged at one end, showed the nature of the explosive. The whole front of the building was shattered to kindling wood. Another bomb of the same kind, loaded with dynamite, was found under the dwelling, directly beneath the sleeping-room of Mr. and Mrs. McClintock and two children. The fuse to this had been lighted, but did not burn down to the explosive. Had it been discharged the building and the whole family would have been blown to pieces. The shock of the bomb bursting threw Mr. and Mrs. McClintock out of bed and wrecked the interior of the house. The country for miles around is aroused. The town council held a meeting soon after daybreak and offered a reward of $5,000 for information that would lead to the detection of the criminal. McClintock was counsel for the anti-license crusaders in Union, and as prosecuting attorney in recent criminal cases had made many enemies. A German baker named Koehler has been arrested on suspicion. A crowd tried to take him from the officer to lynch him. Koehler is thirty-five years old and is wanted in New York state as a fugitive from justice. In February, 1873, he was convicted of burglary in Orange County and sent to Sing Sing prison for five years. In June of the same year he escaped. He has been doing business as a baker in Union City for five years. He was indicted last February for keeping a disorderly house and Mr. McClintock prosecuted him at that time. Koehler says McClintock placed the bombs and fired one to make it appear that he is a martyr in the cause of law and order.

EVIDENCE AGAINST KOEHLER.

A dispatch from Erie last night says: Tracks were discovered leading from Koehler's house to the scene of the explosion. Dynamite was found in his possession, and a few days before the attempted assassination of McClintock and his family Koehler bought pipe of the same size as that of which bombs were made. It is known for a certainty now that Koehler knew that McClintock, as the attorney for the Law and Order Society, was about to turn him over to the Sing Sing authorities as a fugitive from justice, he having escaped from that prison in 1873. Koehler admitted his identity.

ADVENTUROUS CAREER OF A MAN WMO SERVED

ADVENTUROUS CAREER OF A MAN WHO SERVED
PART OF A TERM IN SING SING.

Port Jervis, May 6.—In 1873 a young baker of this village named Frank Koehler, was sentenced to five years in Sing Sing on his confession of being the leader of a gang of burglars that had been operating extensively in this and other places along the Erie Railway. Koehler was put to work in the prison cooper shop. Four months after entering the prison, with the aid of fellow convicts, he headed himself up in a barrel, which was carried with others and loaded on a barge bound down the river. At Tarrytown, night having fallen, Koehler let himself out of the barrel, jumped into the river and swam ashore. He broke into a farm house near Tarrytown, changed his prison suit for the farmer's clothes and the next day was in Port Jervis. He went up among the Sulivan County mountains, where he was captured some weeks later. He escaped from the officer, swam the Delaware River to Pennsylvania and was never recaptured. Koehler had a brother in Port Jervis, who, some months later, received a letter from the escaped convict. He was in Rio Janiero, Brazil, having joined the United States Navy and deserted. At the time he wrote he was about shipping as a sailor on a merchant vessel. This vessel was wrecked and Koehler alone escaped. He then worked at his trade in London, married and then came to America. Two or three years ago a man named Koehler appeared in Union City, Erie County, Penn., with his wife and two children. Some weeks ago he was detected while exploding dynamite cartridges in French Creek and destroying large numbers of trout. He fled to a swamp to escape arrest. F. M. McClintock, counsel for the Union City Law and Order Society, took charge of the case. While investigating he learned enough to satisfy him that Koehler was the convict who escaped from Sing Sing in 1873. McClintock took measures to have Koehler handed over to the prison authorities. A few nights ago McClintock's house was demolished by an explosion. Pieces of gas pipe, apparently used as dynamite bombs, were discovered in the ruins. It was learned that Koehler had purchased pipe of that kind the day before the explosion. Tracks were discovered leading from Koehler's house to McClintock's and back again. A warrant was issued for Koehler's arrest, and he was surprised while in his house and captured. PRISONER AT SING SING FIFTEEN YEARS AGO, NOW A PROSPEROUS BAKER IN PENNSYL VANIA-A LAWYER'S EFFORT TO RETURN THE MAN TO A CELL. [BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
PRISONER AT SING SING FIFTEEN YEARS AGO,
NOW A PROSPEROUS BAKER IN PENNSYL-
VANIA—A LAWYER'S EFFORT TO RE-
TURN THE MAN TO A CELL.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

Albany, N. Y., Dec. 5.—Governor Hill had under consideration this afternoon an application for a pardon in a criminal case of more than ordinary interest. Fifteen years ago the farmers of Orange County suffered from a series of burglaries. Finally the constables arrested a gang of thieves and succeeded in obtaining sufficient evidence to convict them of having committed the robberies. One of the thieves was Frank Koehler. He was the youngest of the gang, only nineteen years of age, and it was shown on the trial that he had only recently been drawn into the operations of the gang. Owing to his youth and the fact that he had never before committed a crime, Koehler was sentenced to only five years' imprisonment. Governor Hill said this afternoon that, if the Elmira Reformatory had been in existence, Koehler would have been sent to that institution and not to the State Prison. Koehler had been in Sing Sing Prison only six months when he conceived the idea of escaping. The prison authorities were then making cement and sending that article out of the prison in barrels. Koehler crept into an empty barrel and induced another convict to put the head into the barrel. The barrel was rolled on board a schooner standing at the prison wharf, and soon afterward the schooner started down the Hudson River toward New-York. In the night following, Koehler kicked out the head of the barrel, and jumping into the Hudson River, swam ashore. He made his way to New-York and shipping as a common scaman went to South America. Subsequently he made voyages to England and China. Finally he returned to this country in 1878, and going to Union City, Erie County, Pennsylvania, where his father lived, started in business as a baker. He prospered and now owns the building in which his bakery is situated. He is married and has lived with such apparent honesty that to-day Governor Hill was presented with a petition signed by three-fourths of the inhabitants of Union City praying that he may be pardoned. He had excited the enmity of a man who had him indicted on a petty charge. No evidence to uphold the indictment could be procured by the District-Attorney and accordingly it was dismissed. It was believed that a lawyer named T. M. McClintock had something to do with the indictment, Koehler having signed a petition to the courts to have McClintock disbarred. Soon afterward the house of McClintock was blown up with dynamite. No one was injured, but the house was ruined. McClintock charged that Koehler was guilty of firing the dynamite and Koehler accordingly was arrested and indicted. When the case came up for trial, as the presiding judge wrote to Governor Hill, no evidence was presented that in the slightest degree connected Koehler with the crime. Moreover the District-Attorney moved that the indictment should be quashed. Koehler opposed the granting of the motion, sayfing that he desired to have the case given to a jury. But, of course, there being no evidence to offer against him, the request of the District-Attorney that the indictment should be quashed was granted. McClintock in the meantime had learned that Koehler was an escaped convict. The prison authorities of Sing Sing were informed of the fact and they immediately applied to Governor Hill for a requisition upon the Governor of Pennsylvania for the surrender of the prisoner. The escaped convict was immediately arrested and lodged in the jail at Erie, Pennsylvania. The requisition has been granted by Governor Hill and Governor Beaver, of Pennsylvania, has consented to the surrender of Koehler, but the lawyers for the prisoner have caused delays, hoping to procure a pardon for him from Governor Hill.

To-day Albert B. Osborne, of Corry, Pennsylvania, the counsel of Koehler, appeared before Governor Hill, and appealed to him to grant a pardon to his client. The Governor said that he had received a long letter from McClintock, protesting against the granting of any pardon to Koehler. Governor Hill replied:

"I will take your application for a pardon into serious consideration, Mr. Osborne, and will inform you by telegraph before Monday next of my decision."

Y., Dec. 15.—State Detective James Jackson has returned to Sing Sing prison from Eric, Pa., with Frank Koehler, the man who was arrested as a party concerned in the dynamite outrages at Union City, Pa., last May.
