noah-taylor-harrisonburg-1888-11-30.A11:
CATAHOULA.
Another Assassination.
Information reached this city yesterday of the assassination on Saturday evening last, in Catahoula parish, three miles below Harrisonburg, of Mr. R. N. Stegall, who formerly lived in Natchoz. The report as it came to us, is to the effect that on Saturday last, Mr. Stegall, who has been residing at or near Trinity, went to Harrisonburg on business. He was returning to his home in the afternoon, and when about three miles below Harrisonburg, he was shot by some one in ambush on the roadside, the weapon used being a shot-gun, his right side being torn to pieces by the discharge, and he being knocked off his horse. While in the throes of death his assassin stepped up to him, and, placing a revolver to his forehead, fired two more shots into the dying man's head, thus completing his awful work.

The shots appear to have attracted attention, and the assassin hearing assistance coming, incontinently fled, leaving his shot gun behind, which it is hoped may lead to his identification. Mr. Stegall was a quiet, inoffensive man, and it was not thought that he had an enemy in the world. He lived at one time in Natchez, being the engineer at the ice factory and doing other work here, and was well thought of. He leaves a large family who were entirely dependent upon him for support, and they will perhaps suffer.

While no motive has been ascribed for the crime, there are certain parties suspected (said to have gone over to Cataboula from Natchez,) and they will be arrested when found, if, indeed, they have not already been taken into custody.—Natchez Democrat.

Noah Taylor, a worthless negro living at Harrisonburg, was arrested the day after the murder on suspicion, and the evidence pointing to his guilt, he was taken from jail and lynched by a mob.

Dobie formerly worked in the car-shops, at Pullman, but left town at Christmas, and his wife, who was employed in the Hotel Florence, had not heard from him until this afternoon, when he opened the door of her room and entered, saying, "I've come to see you again." Mrs. Dobie rose from her chair with the remark, "I'm sorry, for you have done nothing to support me, and I wish you would go away, and not annoy me." Beaten by an Old Game. LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 24.—Last Tuesday a stranger entered the shoe shop of V. Hoffman to buy a pair of shoes. A moment later another man came in, and appearing to know the first, offered him a box of diamonds, he was forced to sell. They struck a bargain, and the first-comer paid $100 in cash. They went out together, the first man taking a pair of shoes to try. A few hours later the seller returned, and said he had found a jeweler who would pay him $250 for the stones. robert-gibson-barnesville-1888-05-24.A3:
A HANGING BEE SPOILED.
The Barnesville Fiend Speeded Away by the Authorities
TO PREVENT HIS LYNCHING,
Which Would Certainly Have Taken Place--Depravity that Seems to be a Family Trait--A Very Indignant Mob.
Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.

BARNESVILLE, O., May 25.—Bob Gibson, the negro who assaulted the child Minnie Jefferson, yesterday was not lynched, the mob being content with giving him a most terrible beating. He waived examination to-day before Justice Baker and was taken to jail. The excitement over the horrible affair had quieted down considerably this morning, but broke out afresh this afternoon, when it was learned that Minor Gibson, a brother of Bob, had been arrested on the charge of exposing his person to a number of highly respectable country ladies. This low wretch also waived examination and accompanied his brother to jail. The prompt action of the authorities in speeding the brutes away spoiled a hanging bee which would undoubtedly have taken place had they remained here a few hours longer. To-night the town is quiet and the community has a relief from the excitement of the past twenty-four hours.

The particulars of Bob Gibson's arrest and punishment by a mob last night are as follows:

AN INDIGNANT PEOPLE.

About noon Gibson was seen with the child in the rear of the First National Bank building, by one of the attaches of the bank, who reported the matter to his associates of the bank, who made further investigation. Enough was seen to convince them of Gibson's design, and the case was at once reported. The news spread rapidly, and in a short time a band of indignant citizens were hunting for him. In the meantime a warrant for his arrest was sworn out by the father of the child, and Gibson was arrested on the railroad. a short distance east of town, and brought in and placed in the lockup. The excitement began to grow rapidly, and by evening the feeling against him became intense, and threats to take him out, "hang him," "whip him," "tar and feather him," etc., were openly made. It was announced that the preliminary trial would not take place till morning, and later the report came that Gibson had waived an examination, and would be taken to the county jail in the morning. These reports only served to intensify the feeling against the prisoner, and it came to be generally believed that Gibson would be roughly handled before morning.

TAKEN BY A MOB.

Constables Bulger and Renner were on guard at the lockup. About dark, there were seen to gather little groups of men about City Hall, and the signs of an intent on the part of the mob to get Gibson became more ominous. Everything was quiet and orderly until a few minutes after 11 o'clock, when a small band of men were seen to cross the street to City Hall from the opposite side. In a short time Frank Jeffries, the father of the girl, made this announcement: "Gentlemen, here I am, who will protect me?" "All of us," came the response from a hundred determined men. A grand rush was then made through the Mayor's office and out into the jail yard. Constable Bulger single-handed was powerless to repel the mob, and in a short time the work of battering down the barred door with sledge and prys commenced and within twenty minutes from the start an entrance was effected, and Gibson, terribly frightened, was in their hands. He was hustled out, and through the streets to Bradfield's lot east of town and

GIVEN A WHIPPING.

Upon arriving at the place of "execution," amid shouts of "hang'im!" "cut his throat!" "whip him!" etc., a consultation was held to determine which of the above would be the best means of punishment. After several motions it was finally decided that Gibson should be completely thrashed. After several minutes delay he was stripped and the whipping began. A number of beech switches was procured and the culprit, tied to a tree with a pair of suspenders, took his medicine with the bravery of a Spartan. The "judge" then decided that the prisoner be returned to jail without further molestation, and his deputies acted accordingly. Once more at the jail the prisoner was delivered to Marshal Renner, who locked him up for "safe keeping." Upon examination Gibson's back and head were found to be severely bruised and cut, but with some attention his wounds will be healed in a few days.

Since the arrest of Gibson on this charge, his general bad reputation for depravity of this kind has been reviewed. It is charged that several other little white girls of the town have fallen victims to his practices. His plan was to entice the children into secluded places and by giving them candy and money, induce them to submit to nameless indignities.

Special Telegram to the Register.

BARNESVILLE, O, May 25.—The town is quiet to-night. Gibson, the black wretch, waived examination before Justice Baker to-day and is now in the county jail. robert-gibson-barnesville-1888-05-24.A6:
A BRUTE FLOGGED.
A Negro Taken From Jail and Soundly Thrashed by a Mob.
Thrashed by a Mob.

BARNESVILLE, O., May 26.—The fever of excitement occasioned by the arrest of Robert Gibson, the negro charged with assaulting a little white girl, culminated in a crowd of undisguised citizens overpowering the guard at the lockup; the iron bars were battered down and Gibson was taken out among the deafening shouts of the mob and escorted to the outskirts of the town. The mob took Gibson to a field a short distance west of town, where his fate was put to vote. The proposition to hang him was voted down. It was then proposed to emasculate him, but this failed to carry, when the one to give him a flogging was decided upon. The wretch was then stripped and given an unmerciful beating after which he was escorted back to town and turned over to the authorities. Great excitement prevails. Gibson waived examination and was taken to the county jail yesterday evening.

Excitement is again high over the arrest yesterday of Minor Gibson, a brother of Bob, on the charge of theft and exposure of his person to ladies. He is an ex-Penitentiary bird and a low character. It seems probable that there is severe punishment in store for this last offender, judging from the tone of an incensed community.
robert-gibson-barnesville-1888-05-24.A11:
MOB AT BARNESVILLE.
Barnesville was very greatly agitated on Thursday of last week, by the story of the brutal conduct of a well known negro named Robert Gibson, toward a 5-year-old daughter of Frank Jeffries, of that place. About noon Gibson was seen in the vicinity of an outhouse in the rear of the First National Bank, with the child, and they were observed to enter the building. The report gained credence that the purposes of the lustful negro was to debauch the child, and the public indignation became intense. However, the fellow paraded the streets for some time, as if his act of enticing the child for any purpose was a very proper thing, and he was unmolested by the crowd who afterward set the officers of the law at defiance. A warrant was finally sworn out by the father of the child, and placed in the hands of Marshal Renner. Gibson was arrested by W. H. Brown, a deputy, a short distance east of town, and taken back to the lockup, where he was guarded by Officers Renner and John Buiger. About 11 o'clock the same evening a mob of possibly fifty or a hundred men, headed by some half-dozen well known "negro haters," made a rush upon the jail in the temporary absence of Officer Renner, who had gone to get a lunch, and overpowered Bulger, and with sledges began battering down the door of the jail. Renner put in an appearance before the work was completed, and plied his mace vigorously, but he too was overpowered and roughly used, and given to understand that his protection of the prisoner would be at his own peril. Finally the destruction of the door was accomplished and the prisoner secured. He was hustled through the streets to a lot near town, where, amid the cries of the excited crowd, "hang him," "shoot him," "cut his throat," and the like, it was determined to whip him. He was stripped and tied to a tree, and his body was lacerated by a bullet of beech wives, and he was otherwise severely punished, and returned to the lockup, where the officers of the law were kindly permitted to keep him in custody. The next day a brother of the man, named Minor Gibson, who was charged with indecently exposing his person, was arrested, and the twain were brought to jail in this place.

The Grand Jury investigated carefully both the cases and failed to find any evidence upon which to base an indictment against Bob Gibson, the man about whom the mobites flew into such a fine frenzy.

The negro was doubtless guilty of a wrong against society, and his action in decoying an innocent child was an outrage—it was bestial, deserving of the severest censure and punishment, yet the action of the mob in defying law cannot be tolerated. It was the duty of the officers to protect the prisoner, and the men who set at defiance their authority set themselves up against the authority of the State—as court and jury. Belmont county cannot afford to be governed by such law, and the Grand Jury has so found.

Hugh J. Campbell's call for a general convention of Dakota Divisionists will be issued in a few days and will be for 700 delegates to meet at Huron July 10 to 12. Other conventions of special interest will closely follow, to take measures looking to the same end.

In Pickens county, Chickasaw Nation, Indian Territory, non-residents are opposing the collection of the tax on stock, and have organized and armed themselves with Winchesters. The militia is unable to cope with them, and the aid of the United States will be invoked by the tribal authorities. General warfare is feared.

Mormons have been having a five days' jubilee at Manti, San Pete County, Utah, dedicating their third temple in the Territory, and claim that great signs and wonders attended the ceremonies, angel voices singing around the heads of the speakers, and the appearance of the spirits of Presidents Brigham Young, John Taylor, and J. M. Grant.

At 3 o'clock Wednesday morning a freight train on the Rock Island railroad went through a bridge near Randolph, Mo., crashing into a revine twenty-five feet deep. A short time after a freight on the Hannibal & St. Joseph went through a bridge which adjoined the Rock Island, and which had been weakened by the first wreck. A brakeman, an engineer, and two tramps were killed, a fireman fatally injured and two other train men badly hurt.

Farmer Greenwood, living near Curtis, Neb., Wednesday shot and killed his daughter, Mrs. Annie Bryant, a few minutes after she had given birth to a child, and tried to kill the child, but his wife saved it. Greenwood's daughter was only 17 years old, and had been married but three months. Her husband had been forced to marry her to escape criminal proceedings, and soon after deserted her. Greenwood was moody, and it is supposed made partially insane by his daughter's shame.

The several policy shops at Evansville, Ind., are crying fraud because players at each resort Wednesday night played the same combination and it won all around to the extent of $10,000.

Fuller reports of the cyclone which swept over Brownton, Texas, Tuesday, state that the Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian churches were demolished, and eight houses were destroyed, one of them being carried some distance, and its occupant, Amanda Willis (colored), instantly killed. The path of the storm was 300 feet wide, and crops, buildings, trees, fences, and everything in the danger belt were swept away.

At the sixty-seventh session of the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted Masons of Indiana, at Indianapolis Tuesday, Isaac P. Leyden, of New Albany, was elected Grand Master.

Governor Martin, of Kansas, Tuesday pardoned Charles B. Rotrock, under life sentence for killing his wife while under the influence of liquor, attaching to the pardon a condition unheard of before in this State, that Rotrock forever abstain from the use of intoxicating liquors. If Rotrock should violate the condition he could be reimprisoned on an order from the Governor.

The thirtieth annual meeting of the Illinois State Sunday School Convention was opened at Rockford Wednesday afternoon.

The Wisconsin Unitarian Conference opened its semi-annual session at Janesville Tuesday.

W. L. Bancroft, of Port Huron, Mich., has been appointed general superintendent of the railway mail service, vice T. E. Nash, resigned. Mr. Bancroft has accepted the appointment and will enter upon the duties of his office June 1.

Judgments amounting to $22,000 were rendered against the Illinois Central Railroad Company at Bloomington, Ill., Monday, in the Cobb-Christy cases, which have been on trial for twenty-five years, growing out of losses on grain shipped South during the war on that road by delay in transportation, the company claiming that the delay was caused by the government holding control of the road. Appeals will be taken.

BELLAIRE, O., June 14.—Six of the Barnesville parties indicted by the grand jury for taking Robert Gibson, the colored man, charged with attempted rape of a little girl, and thrashing him, are Francis Jeffries, the girl's father, W. H. Brown, Jonathan Ellis, Sol Morris, Asa Browers and Frank Moore. They were arraigned in court, entered pleas of not guilty, and gave bond in the sum of $200 each. The penalty for this offense is a fine of not more than $500 and imprisonment of not more than sixty days. Gibson is now working in this city. Coal Men in Confab.
CLEVELAND, O., June 14.—The Western Coal Dealers' association is in session here, and it is reported that a drop of $1, if no more, per ton will be agreed upon as the summer rate. There are rumors of a serious disaffection among the members constituting the combine at the action taken during the past winter by the coal barons of Pennsylvania in needlessly forcing up prices and compelling the western dealers to unjustly bear the brunt and public reprobation which this conduct called forth.

Millions of Bandanas.

PROVIDENCE, R. I., June 14.—Since the St. Louis nominations the Clyde print works here have received orders for 2,000,000 bandana handkerchiefs and have put on 300 extra hands, who, with this large force are working night and day to turn them out. Charged with Seducing His Pupils.
OWENSBORO, Ky., March 9.—Robert Hardin, a colored school teacher at Utica, this county, is charged with the seduction of nearly all the girls in his school. Amanda Pry, aged 15, will die. Hardin gave her medicine to produce abortion. Miss Harlowe gave birth to a child four days ago and died Wednesday. She confessed that John Van Maeter was the father of the child. That individual, together with Hardin, has skipped for parts unknown.
robert-hardin-utica-1888-03-14.A3:
A Beastly School Teacher.
EVANSVILLE, March 8.—[Special.]—At Utica, a small village near Owensboro, Ky., a prepossessing young colored girl, Amanda Pry, the daughter of a well-to-do colored farmer, died to-day from the effects of an attempted abortion. On her death bed she confessed that Robert Hardin. her school master was her seducer and that five other pupils were enciente, being the result of Hardin's lost. After the death of the young girl Hardin escaped. A posse was organized and will lynch him if found which will probably be before morning.
robert-hardin-utica-1888-03-14.A4:
Peck's Bad Boy.
OWENSBORO, Ky., March 9.—A series of crimes committed by a colored school teacher near here has aroused that race to a frenzy. Near Utica there is a colored school taught by a young negro, Robert Hardin. Among the pupils is a girl of fifteen years, Amanda Pry, daughter of Henry Pry, a very wealthy colored farmer. Some months ago the teacher betrayed the girl, and when the evidence of their sin became apparent he at once set about producing malpractice. Finding that something was wrong with his daughter, the father questioned her and she confessed everything. He was advised to have Hardin arrested, and he came to Owensboro for that purpose, but Hardin took the alarm when the old man left home, and packed his traps and left for parts unknown. The girl died today after making the startling disclosure that six other girls in the school, aged from thirteen to sixteen years, were in a similar condition and had been regularly drugged by the villian to destroy the existence of his crimes. A lynching party is now in hot pursuit of Hardin.

The attendance in the branch (colored) schools of Cincinnati, O., has exceeded the expectations of the many teachers engaged in them. Judson, of Colton, Cal., addressed the colored Republican club of Hot Springs, Ark., on the issues of the day. After leaving the hall he was assaulted by three white men, knocked down and stabbed. Jacksonville, Ill., society has been convulsed by a social sensation. Miss Hattie Flack, daughter of Chas. E. Flack, of the firm of Schrewin & Flack, commission merchants, has married one John Sams, a coal black Negro and her father's hired man. The way they do it down South: A pair of white church goers met a pair of colored church goers on a plank walk at Utica, Miss. They were going in opposite directions. Because the colored pair did not give up the sidewalk entirely, the white man put his hands on the shoulder of the colored woman to push her off. The colored man resented this. Next day "the intention was to give the Negro a sound thrashing and then let him go." The Negro refused to be thrashed. Result, a white man shot down dead in self defense, and a Negro lynched.

A Mr. Smith, of England, is creating quite a sensation among white society of Atlanta, Ga., by visiting at the home of the Rev. C. R. Carter, pastor of the largest colored church in that city. Mr. Smith is a traveled young man of thirty, and the son of a large blanket manufacturer of Halifax. He has been in India and visited almost every part of the world. When Mr. Carter was in England this summer, Smith took him to his house and treated him as one of the family, hence the present visit is simply an exchange of courtesies.

James Shells, of New York, is a boss bricklayer and contractor, and the only man of color belonging to the union of mechanics of that profession there. He is a young man, about twenty-six years of age, and is making rapid strides in North Carolina, where he learned his trade. He had to board himself on $150 a year, or fifty cents per day. In New York he demanded five dollars per day, and recently he passed a Civil Service Board examination, and has been appointed inspector of the Great Aqueduct at a salary of $2,100. It is, without a doubt, one of the greatest pieces of engineering and masonry work ever attempted in the city. It is a large tunnel, 200 feet in circumference, 100 feet in diameter, and is fifty miles long, extending from Croton Lake to New York City.

SHE MARRIED THE NEGRO COACHMAN, AND HE HAS PROBABLY BEEN LYNCHED.

Says a special to the Philadelphia Press from St. Louis, Oct. 1: D.C. McCoy, a deputy sheriff, who left Jacksonville, Ill., last week on the trail of Press Sams, the negro who was married to a white woman, Miss Hattle Flack, about two weeks ago, near Jacksonville, arrived with the woman in his custody and turned her over to her father, Charles E. Flack, of Schreiver, Flack & Co. commission merchants, of this city. McCoy, who is an old friend of the family, found the couple at a log cabin in the mountains, near Clinton, living with the family of Sams' brother-in-law. The girl at first refused to go with McCoy, until he convinced her that Sams had another wife from whom he had never been divorced. McCoy refuses to say what became of Sams, but intimates that he was lynched to save the state the expense of his trial for bigamy. The report given out at Clinton is that Sams has left the country. The Flack family live near Jacksonville, and Sams was their coachman.
sama.A7:
Hattie Flack's Repentance.
St. Louis, Oct. 1.—Hattie Flack, the nineteen-year old daughter of Charles Flack, of the St. Louis commission firm of Shriner & Flack, who married a mulatto named Pres Sams, the hired man on her father's farm, near Jacksonville, Ill., is at home again. She was brought to St. Louis and turned over to her parents by Deputy Sheriff McCoy, of Jacksonville, who found her near Moscow, Ky. Sams fled and escaped lynching. It transpires that the negro was a married man when he induced Miss Flack to wed him. The girl now bitterly repents her folly.
sama.A11:
Miss Flack's Infatuation.
CLINTON, Ky., Oct. 2.—Miss Flack, the daughter of a St. Louis merchant, who married Press Sams, a negro, at Jacksonville, Ills., a short time ago, who has since deserted her, was arrested at Moscow, Saturday night, in the house of Jim Gholson, a negro brother-in-law of Press Sams. Two Negroes Suffer for Insulting Ladies in Wilkes County, Georgia.

[SPECIAL TO THE EVENING WORLD.]

ELBERTON, Ga., Dec. 1.—News has just reached here from Wilkes County of the drowning of two colored men by a posse of citizens.

On Tuesday night Tim Smith and John Coleman were taken from their home and drowned in the river.

Hulda Coleman, wife of one of the drowned men. and Jim Smith, brother of Tim, were severely whipped and notified to leave the place.

The negroes had been insulting white ladies and had also made threats of shooting and burning-out respectable citizens.
tim-smith-washington-1888-11-27.A3:
Shocking Tragedy in Georgia. ATLANTA, Dec. 1.—In Wilkes county, on the Broad River, and near the Lincoln county line, on Thursday, Mrs. Jane Bramlett, during the absence of her husband, was insulted by two negroes. Tim Smith and John Coleman. When officers sought to arrest them they resisted by firing upon them. Three hundred armed men then visited the place and a young white man, who was suspected of having incited the negroes, had to flee the county to escape the vengeance of the mob. The two negroes were thrown into the river with rocks tied to them. No effort has been made to recover their bodies. The negroes are aroused, and have armed themselves. The whites have appealed to Gov. Gordon for protection. Browned in a Mill Pond.
NYACK. Dec. 1.—On Monday last Frederick Degener of Garnerville, a widower, 65 years old, worked for Farmer Millspaugh killing hogs. That night two men named Tripear and Hinds, while passing the mill pond of the Garnerville print works, heard a splash, but a search revealed nothing. Yesterday a Mr. Coeman discovered Degener's body in two feet of water. Subsequent evidence shows that Degener doubtless fell in the pond while intoxicated.

At the Atlanta university there have been within the past three weeks twenty-two cases of fever, three of which have been typhoid and the others malarial. Of the twenty-two there were three cases to result fatally, one teacher and two pupils. The illness followed closely the republican celebration and jubilee, in which all the pupils participated, exposing themselves for hours in the damp, cold night air. To this exposure the illness is ascribed, more especially since the new cases are reported. Dr. Manahan, the physician in charge of most of the cases, superintended a thorough examinations of the buildings, grounds and wells and is positive that the sickness can be ascribed to no local cause. At any rate, the sickness is over. None but the three cases were serious at all and those still on the sick list are in no danger.

Americus Republican: A young woman in an adjoining county, who had an eye on a young farmer, found that he was a pretty strong democrat, and proposed to bet herself against himself that Harrison would be elected. The young man kicked against the bet, saying he did not need a wife, but as she insisted he finally said, "well, as Cleveland is sure to elected, I'll take the bet and make you wait till I get ready to take you." "All right, said the girl, "and if Harrison is elected, you've got to marry me on inaugural day or give me your farm." The young chap agreed to this, but since found out that the supposed young lady was nearly twenty years older than himself, and he has turned over the farm to a creditor and left for Texas. The woman proposes to follow as soon as she can locate him, and claim her husband, as she says she "ain't gwine to be cheated this late in life out of the only chance she ever had to git a man."

Newnan Heraid: The special term of Coweta superior court, appointed for the first week in December, to try the railroad cases, will not be held. On Wednesday last Col P. F. Smith, leading counsel for plaintiffs, received a proposition from the attorneys of the Atlanta and West Point railroad looking to a compromise. Col. Smith went to Atlanta in response to the summons, and as a result of the conference thus brought about, a compromise was effected, and the cases were all dismissed, including that of Felix Dickson, which is now pending in the supreme court. By the terms of the settlement Col. Smith and his associates receive $5,500, the gentlemen associated with him in the case being Messrs. P. S. Whatley, P. H. Brewster, and Willcoxon & Wright. It was not as fat a fee as they might have obtained had the cases been followed up, but they did not want to be too hard on the railroad company, and generously agreed to compromise. The trial of the cases would have occupied about a week, and their dismissal saves the county about $700 in the matter of court expenses.

Ed Thompson is a young negro, who has been carrying the bi-weekly mail from Gainesville to Cumming for sometime past. Friday, on arriving at the postoffice at Pleasant Grove, which is situated about sixty yards from Mr. Blackstock's residence, he found no one in the office, the door was locked but the key was on the outside. The negro went in the office, found two registered packages lying on the shelf, secured them, and went out, locking the door behind him. He then called the postmaster and delivered the mail sack. Mr. Blackstock changed the mail, but did not miss the letters then, but did soon after Thompson left. When the theft was discovered suspicion naturally rested on Thompson and G. Rice went in immediate pursuit, arriving in Gainesville an hour after the negro did. Securing the services of Marshal Hanie the negro was traced up and captured on a street car, his intention doubtless being to leave town. When accused he confessed to the deed and produced the money, amounting to $105, less 65 cents, which he had spent. He was carried before United States Commissioner Gaston and bound over in default of bond. The penalty attached to this offense is a fine of not more than $1,000 and by imprisonment at hard labor for not more that five years.

Lincolnton News: We have been reliably informed that near Delhi, in Wilkes county, on one day last week some negroes, on the plantation of a Mr. Bramlett, in his absence, approached his wife and demanded the keys to the cotton house. Upon her refusal they drew their pistols and threatened to shoot Mrs. Bramlett and daughter unless the keys were delivered to them. Under these threats Mrs. Bramlett prudently gave them up. After securing the keys to the cotton house the negroes loaded up a wagon with seed cotton, and carried it to a store near by and sold it. As soon as the surrounding neighbors learned of the audacity of these miscreants they determined to arrest and punish them. They, the negroes, knowing that this high handed outrage of theirs would be punished as soon as found out, armed themselves with guns and fled to the woods, defying arrest, by the legal authorities. The whites of the neighborhood having their indignations aroused by the brutal treatment of Mrs. Bramlett and daughter by these black scoundrels, determined at all hazzards to arrest the guilty parties. For this purpose a "posse comitatus" was organized and a scouring of the woods began. In the meantime it was rumored that the negroes of the neighborhood were organizing themselves with the intention of defending and preventing the violators of the law from being arrested. The excitement is running very high, and unless these ignorant and misguided people disband at once, a terrible retribution will be melted out to them. It is rumored that one negro has already been killed or fatally wounded. We await events from that section with considerable anxiety.

FLORIDA.

Quite a number of people are expected at Chipley from the north next month.

The Lake City correspondent of the News wrote as follows Nov. 30: The heaviest frost of the season; this morning ice formed as thick as a knife blade in exposed places out doors. It is rumored that Robert Hatcher died of yellow fever this morning at Olustee, Fla. J. Bradford of Tallahassee has been appointed director of the agricultural experiment station of Florida, vice J

The action of the democratic governors of Tennessee, Maryland and North Carolina granting certificates to the candidates, who have a majority on the face of the returns, has settled the lower House of Congress beyond all doubt in favor of the republicans by a majority of 7. The governors named might have with considerable reason withheld the certificates to the republicans, because of the irregularities, but they are democrats and would take no semblance of an advantage over an enemy. The horns and tail having gone with the hide to the republicans, it will be interesting to observe what they will do with them. There is one thing certain, the surplus will go.

GEN. CHALMERS, the renegade Mississippiian, who was beaten for Congress by about 8,000 votes at the recent election, has gone to Washington to lay the foundation for a contest. En route he stopped at Indianapolis to pay his respects to Harrison and urge the appointment of Mahone to a cabinet position. Mahone is a natural born thief and Chalmers is a scoundrel from choice, so there is no wonder that there is a mutual admiration between them.

The municipal election at Frankfort passed without the disturbance expected after a very heated and bitter campaign, and resulted in the re-election of E. H. Taylor mayor, over Ex-Chief Justice Alvin Duvall by a majority of 65. Taylor has a distillery and the old man hasn't, which may account for the milk in the cocoanut.

Mr. Carlisle and other leading members of Congress are for the immediate admission of all the Territories that are eligible to Statehood. The democrats in the House have it in their power in the next three months to take the initiative in this matter and it is to be hoped that they will apply themselves at once to the task.

HUMMY WILLSON, the fellow who ran against Caruth for congress and was snowed under by 3,000 or 4,000 majority, wanted to keep himself in further notice by demanding a re-count of the vote, but the governor went right along and issued the certificate of election to Caruth without noticing the demand.

Let's see. Wisconsin was one of those States which credulous democrats claimed might go for Cleveland. The returns show how badly they were deceived, for Harrison not only carries it, but does so by 6,591 over Blaine's, his plurality being 21,271. This is one of those misses that is equal to many miles.

The exact democratic majority in Kentucky on Cleveland electors is 28,666, it is at last officially announced. The prohibition vote is 5,221, the labor 622 and Belva Lockwood 2. The prohibitionists gain 2,119 over the vote of St. John and lose 3,177 as against Fox for governor in 1887.

Isn't it about time the newspapers were catching on to the way to spell Congressman-elect Goodknight's surname? His brother, T. M., postmaster at Franklin, told us several years ago that the last sylable commenced with a "k" and as he is an "educator" he ought to know.

Here is a warning to gum masticators. Mary Murphy, sweet 16, of Newtown, Conn., went to sleep chewing a piece, which slipped down her throat, lodged in the entrance to the stomach and caused a fatal ulceration.

STATE pride did not ent as big a figure in Indiana as it might. Harrison ran bedind Hovey 150 votes, the majorities for both of whom were secured through the most flagrantly fraudulent practices imaginable.

The democratic majority on Congressmen this year in Kentucky is more than three times greater than in 1886, when it was but 10,882.

—We haven't got much of a navy to brag of, but it cost $23,003,624 this year and the secretary wants $26,767,697 for next.

NEWS CONDENSED.

—Seth N. Ramsey committed suicide with a shotgun at Midway.

—One would hardly believe it, but it is said we still have 265,000 Indians with us.

—McKinley, of Ohio, has the deadwood on the Speakership of the next House.

—The new city directory gives Lexington 27,066 population, 10,815 of whom are negroes.

—John Henry Meyer was hanged at Placerville, Cal., for the murder of a ranchman named Lowell.

—Dr. Hourigan got a change of venue from Marion to Taylor and was taken back to jail at Louisville.

—In West Virginia the prohibition amendment was defeated by 35,574 majority. Only two counties in the State favored it.

—Without government or State aid the Virginia Exposition managers made a complete success of their exhibition and cleared $40,000 for its guarantors.

The American Forestry Congress will meet in Atlanta, Ga., on the 5th, 6th and 7th of December.

Gov. Beaver has accepted the invitation to act as marshal of the inaugural parade on the 4th of March.

Hronek, the anarchist who plotted to blow up several Chicago officers with dynamite, was given 12 years in the pen.

The first train over the new Louisville, St. Louis and Texas road left Louisville for Owensboro yesterday morning.

Under the new law the Electoral College will not assemble until the 2d Tuesday in January, which falls upon the 8th.

Hon. W. Godfrey Hunter says he will not contest the election of Hon. I. H. Goodknight, his democratic opponent in the 3d Congressional district.

"White Caps" went to the home of Mrs. Anna Jester and her grown daughter, near Sardinia, O., bared their backs and whipped them with switches.

The Director of the Mint, in his annual report, estimates the gold product of the United States for the past year at $33,000,000 and that of silver $53,000,000.

A band of armed men, wearing masks, broke open the jail at Wytheville, Va., and rescued a murderer named Wayman Sutton the night before the day fixed for his execution.

The negro Tom Waltz, who cut off the head of Leroy Smith, white, in Lexington last April and escaped to be tracked to Arizona and captured, was given 19 years in the penitentiary last week.

Lucretia McReynolds, of Jasper, Tennessee, brought suit for damages in the sum of $50,000 against a wealthy farmer named Graham for seduction and breach of promise. A jury gave her $25,000.

—Near Nevada, Mo., George Corb, a school teacher, murdered Miss Ella Wray, with whose mother he boarded. He was placed in jail, where he committed suicide by poison, thus escaping a lynching.

—It is reported in Frankfort that the sureties of Ex-Treasurer Tate sent a lawyer to see him in Europe and obtained from him a promise that he would pay half of his defalcation if they would pay the other half.

—It is reported that the president will appoint Ex-Governor Proctor Knott, of Kentucky, to the vacancy upon the civil service commission made by the promotion of John H. Oberly to the head of the Indian Bureau.

—A couple of negroes went to the house of a white man in Wilkes county, Ga., and insulted his wife in his absence. A mob ran them down and attaching weights to their feet, threw them alive into the river.

—S. T. Leavy, of Woodford, who will be remembered as the man who was fined $30 for telling a juror in the celebrated Munday case at Lexington to hang the old woman, has been appointed Indian agent at Yankton.

—All of the coal mines along the Monongahela river have shut down indelibly. The operators claim that they have been losing money on account of the over-supply. Over 5,000 miners are thus thrown out of employment.

—Mrs. Emma Jackson, of Glasgow, Mo., asked her brother, Harry Ballow, of 14 years, to bring her a bucket of water, which he refused to do. Threatening to whip him, she went after the water herself, and on her return was met at the door by the boy, who fired a gun in her face and killed her.

The controller of the currency reports the organization of 132 National banks during the year and the total number now 3,143, an increase after deducting 34 which went into voluntary liquidation and 8 which failed, of 93. The total capital stock exceeds $592,000,000 and the surplus fund $185,000,000.

Pastor Parker Missing. Oswego, Dec. 4.—The Rev. W. L. Parker, pastor of Christ Episcopa' Church in this city, is missing. His friends have not been able to get any trace of him. RACE WAR IN GEORGIA. Bad Feeling and Bloodshed Among Whites and Blacks.
WASHINGTON, Ga., Dec. 4.—E. B. Cade owns a plantation and runs a store on Broad River, near Danburg. Near him resides J. E. Bramlet, a Baptist clergyman, and his family. On the plantation of Mr. Bramlet lived Tim Smith, a negro tenant, to whom Mr. Cade furnished supplies. Smith was working with Mr. Bramlet for a certain percentage of the crop, and promised to pay Mr. Cade in cotton for the supplies. Cade pressed him for a settlement. The cotton which Smith claimed as his property was stored in the gin house of Mr. Bramlet. On Tuesday last during the absence of Bramlet, Smith went to Mrs. Bramlet and asked for a team with which to deliver the cotton to Cade. Having received instructions from Bramlet before his departure not to allow the cotton removed during his absence, Mrs. Bramlet refused to accede to the request. Smith and his wife both addressed abusive language to Mrs. Bramlet, and Smith went over to Mr. Cade and reported his unsuccessful attempt to secure a team. Mr. Cade furnished Smith with one of his teams and the cotton was hauled over to Cade's.

Mrs. Bramlet swore out a warrant for the arrest of Smith, and a bailiff with a posse went after Smith. The party found Smith with John Coleman and three other negroes, armed and Smith declared that he would die before he would be arrested. The posse managed to secure possession of Smith's gun, when the latter picked up an iron wedge and attacked the officers. He was fired at and seriously wounded. The prisoners were required to furnish bail which was provided by Cade, who abused the officers for arresting Smith and Coleman and threatened to shoot them if they attempted to interfere with them again.

After this a report was circulated that Cade had armed 150 negroes, and the excitement among the whites was great. Arming themselves, they concentrated at the scene of the trouble, but not finding armed negroes they dispersed. Smith and Coleman were in the mean time rearrested for safe keeping.

On Tuesday night a party of forty men went to the stockade, took Smith and Coleman out, and drowned them in Broad River. Mr. Henry Hill learned that danger menaced Mr. Cade, and persuaded him to leave the county. Capt. Gilbert Cade, the father of the young man, says there is no truth in the report that his son furnished arms to the negroes. The lynchers also visited Mrs. Hulden Smith, and whipped her and her brother until they were nearly dead. The negroes are still terribly excited and the whites are in an ugly humor.
tim-smith-washington-1888-11-27.A10:
GEORGIA RACE TROUBLE.
The Drowning of Two Colored Men, and Exciting Results.
WASHINGTON, Ga., Dec. 5.—The negroes along the Red river are still in a state of unrest over the tragedy of last week, while the whites are in an equally ugly humor. The facts of the tragedy, after careful investigation seem to be about as heretofore narrated. Mr. E. B. Cade, a well-connected young man, owns a plantation and runs a store on Broad river, near the village of Danbury. Near him resides Mr. J. E. Bramlet, a Baptist preacher, and his family. On the plantation of Mr. Bramlet lives Tim Smith, a negro tenant, to whom Mr. Cade furnished supplies. Smith was working with Mr. Bramlet for a certain percentage of the crop, and promised to pay Mr. Cade in cotton for the supplies that had been furnished to him by the latter. Mr. Cade pressed him for a settlement. The cotton, which Smith claimed as his property, was stored in the gin house of Mr. Bramlet. On Tuesday last, during the absence of Bramlet, Smith went to Mrs. Bramlet and asked for a team with which to deliver the cotton to Cade. Having received instructions from Bramlet before his departure not to allow the cotton to be removed during his absence, Mrs. Bramlet refused to accede to the request.

On this occasion it is said that Smith and his wife both addressed abusive language to Mrs. Bramlet. During the day Smith went over to the store of Mr. Cade and reported his unsuccessful attempt to procure the team from Mrs. Bramlet. Mr. Cade furnished Smith with one of his teams and the cotton was hauled over to Cade's. Mrs. Bramlet, either through an agent or her brother, swore out a warrant for the arrest of Smith. The warrant was placed in the hands of a bailiff, and, with a posse, they went after Smith. When the party arrived, they found Smith, together with John Coleman and three other negroes armed, and Smith declared that he would die before he would be arrested.

The posse managed to secure possession of Smith's gun, when the latter picked up an iron wedge and made an attack upon the officers. He was fired upon by the man who had gotten possession of the gun and was seriously wounded. The arrest of Smith and Coleman was then effected. The prisoners were carried before the magistrate and they were required to furnish bail for their appearance before a higher court.

Their bonds were signed by Mr. Cade and the negroes were liberated. Mr. Cade abused the officers for arresting Smith and Coleman, and threatened to shoot them if they attempted to interfere with them again. After this a report was circulated that Mr. Cade had armed 150 negroes for the purpose of violence. Excitement among the whites was intense, and arming themselves they concentrated at the scene of the trouble. Finding nothing to arouse suspicion of an outbreak, the vigilance committee dispersed. Smith and Coleman were in the meantime rearrested and placed in the convict stockade of Mr. Henry Hill for safe keeping.

On Tuesday night a party of forty men went to the stockade and took Smith and Coleman out and drowned them in Broad river. Another report is to the effect that the negroes were shot, and still another that they were taken from the stockade and concealed. Before the negroes were disposed of the lynchers visited the home of Mr. Cade, with what exact purpose is not known.

Mr. Henry Hill learned of the danger that menaced Mr. Cade, and persuaded him to leave the country. At the very time that the party were at the home of Mr. Cade he and Mr. Hill were out in the plantation of the former, and occupied a position from which they could observe every movement of the searching party. Mr. Cade wanted to go back to the house, with the hope of vindicating himself, but was dissuaded from doing so by Mr. Hill. Mr. Cade was warned to leave the state, and has since been in Augusta. Sentiment runs very high against him, though he has a large number of friends who exonerate him from any intentional wrong doing. Capt. Gilbert Cade, of Washington, the father of the young gentleman, states that there is no truth in the report that his son furnished arms to the negroes, as he was accused of doing.

It is also reported that the gentleman admitted having provided them with arms, but it was with the intention of protecting their lives in case they were attacked by a mob. What Mr. Cade is censured for most is in permitting Smith to remove his cotton from the gin house of Mr. Bramlet during his absence.

There was no good feeling between the two men. About a year and a half ago Mr. Cade testified on the witness stand that he would not believe Bramlet on oath, and the latter has ever since cherished a feeling of ill will against the young man. Mr. Cade owns fine property and has always borne an unimpeachable reputation. The people of Wilkes do not endorse the drowning of Smith and Coleman, and are in favor of a full investigation of the affair. The lynchers also visited Mrs. Hulden Smith and whipped her and her brother.

tim-smith-washington-1888-11-27.A12:
IT IS MR. CADE'S TURN TO KILL. His Mortal Foe, Mr. Bramlett, Has Just Drowned Two of His Adherents.
ATLANTA, Ga., Dec. 6.—The drowning of the two negroes, Tim Smith and John Coleman, and the brutal whipping of Hulda Smith and Jim Smith by a lynching party were the results of a feud between two white men in Wilkes County. A well-to-do farmer named Bramlett had a quarrel about two years ago with a man named Cade, who operates the local cotton-gin. Early last week, while Bramlett was absent, Tim Smith and John Coleman went to his house and were impudent to his wife. Mrs. Bramlett complained to her husband, who rallied his neighbors to punish the negroes.

An encounter took place in which the negroes made successful resistance. Mr. Cade undertook their defense and gathered them at his house to defend it against the threatened attack of Bramlett's men. For this act Bramlett denounced him, and when the lynchers were organized it was their purpose to put Cade out of the way as well as the suspected negroes. Cade was notified in time and fled the country. The two negroes were given refuge in the penitentiary stockade of Mr. Henry Hills, but they were taken therefrom, carried to the bank of Broad River at a point where a bluff rises twenty feet above the water's level, and after being weighed down with stones were thrown in. The mob then visited the home of the Smiths and lashed Hulda Smith and Jim Smith.
tim-smith-washington-1888-11-27.A15:
AN AWAKENING CONSCIENCE.
A Southern Newspaper Severely Denounces a Recent Lynching of Negroes.

Augusta Chronicle.

We have already published and commented upon the dastardly outrages reported last week near Danburg, in this State. The report states that two negro men were drowned in the river, and two others cruelly whipped. It is not charged that the men were guilty of crimes involving moral turpitude, or of so gross a nature as to call for summary punishment. It appears that the difficulty arose by the instigation of white men who were in some way concerned in a dispute about farm products.

With the government in the full control of our own people and party, with the courts open, with the officers of the law of our own appointment, and the juries of our own selection, and with no chance whatever for the lawless or the guilty to escape punishment for their crimes, a resort to summary vengeance, even for the gravest offenses, is to be deplored and condemned. Lynch law should never be resorted to where good government prevails. If the maddened and cruel mob is to be substituted for the judge and jury, let our temples of justice be closed and draped in mourning.

It pains us to write these words, and we shall hasten to take them back if we have been misinformed as to the facts. The barbarities in Wilkes last week (the drowning of two negro men and the severe whipping of two others) are crimes against civilization and Christianity.

It was an act of barbarism that calls for the prompt punishment of the lawless and inhuman men concerned. This is such a heinous crime against the lives, rights and liberties of the people as to call for prompt action on the part of Governor Gordon. Lynch law should be stamped out in Georgia. The lynchers should be made to suffer the full punishment of the law for their inhuman conduct and outrageous crimes, which language fails us to adequately denounce and condemn.
tim-smith-washington-1888-11-27.A19:
GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
NEWS OF THE TWO STATES TOLD IN PARAGRAPHS.
A North Georgia School Teacher Charged With Robbing His Father of $3,800—An Interesting Fight Over the Property of a Negro Who Was Once a Slave—An Arm Torn off by a Planer.

GEORGIA.

Methodist and Baptist churches are in course of erection at Calhoun.

M. Nussbaum of Macon has decided to close out his business in Talbotton.

J. F. Mathis, at Lincolnton, lost a gin-house and ten bales of cotton Wednesday night by fire.

Frank Bowart, who works at Haiman's slow factory at Atlanta, had one of his arms torn off by a planer Thursday.

At Washington, Thursday, E. A. Barnett's ginhouse and twenty-five bales of cotton and 5,000 bushels of seed were burned.

The Macon public library has made arrangement with Prof. Ira Fisk to give a grand balloon ascension and parachute jump on or about Christmas day.

Charles D. Haines, who recently resigned the presidency of the Macon dummy line, has purchased the Kinderbrook lake park for $50,000. It is the picnic and excursion ground for Albany and Troy, N. Y.

At Atlanta Thursday 115 students of the technological school presented Dr. I. S. Hopkins, the president, with a very handsome gold-headed cane, which they had purchased with a purse made up among themselves.

Maj. J. F. Hanson of Macon has been invited to attend the Tariff League banquet to be given at Delmonico's, New York, on Jan. 17, and respond to the toast, "The southern industrial growth the strongest bond of union and peace."

The Phillip & Wright warehouse at Cedartown was burned Thursday morning at 2 o'clock, together with an adjoining building of small value. The warehouse contained the outfit of the Guardian, which was partly covered by insurance.

Since the Hebrew fair at Atlanta closed the accounts have been balanced, and President Joe Hersch is smiling—smiling because the fair cleared about $8,000. Eight thousand dollars is enough to furnish the orphan asylum, and that was just what the fair was intended for.

Rome *Tribune*: A prominent citizen of Rome on Wednesday sent his son-in-law, in a town not 1,000 miles distant, a telegram worded as follows: "Isaiah ix. 6—first clause—All is well." Let the *Tribune* readers search the scriptures and find the reason the telegram so worded, was sent.

Week before last Allen Hewlett, of Telfair county, was thrown from his horse upon a snag, which penetrated through his mouth on both sides, tearing his mouth open, breaking his teeth and terribly lacerating his chin and mouth. It is a frightful looking wound, which will disfigure him for life.

A little negro child was burned to death on the plantation of W. E. Graham, four miles from McAe, last week. Its mother left it alone in the house for a few mome ts. While she was gone it crawled into the fire, its clothing caught on fire, and it was so badly burned that it died in a short while thereafter.

The republicans of Lee county have made the following nominations: For clerk superior court, James Morgan; for coroner, Warren Paxion; for sheriff, E. B. Martin; for treasurer, T. M. Booker; for tax receiver, J. T. Furgeson; for tax collector, R. A. Forrester; for ordinary, George C. Edwards; for surveyor, S. B. Smith.

Capt. R. E. Park of Macon says: "I have just received a letter from Mrs. Jefferson Davis, who writes me that Mr. Davi weighs 140 pounds, more than she has ever known to weigh. She says he is too feeble to get about much, but his mind is as clear as sunshine, and, despite his four score years, still takes a deep interest in national affairs.

Some of the posse who were summoned by Sheriff Calloway for the purpose of dragging Broad river in Wilkes county, to ascertain if the bodies of the two negroes who were said to have been drowned could be found, have returned. They very carefully dragged the river in the vicinity where the drowning is said to have occurred, but could discover no trace of them.

The case of the Ashley Phosphate Company of Charleston, S. C., vs, J. H. McKenzie & Co., was tried at Augu ta Monday. The result was a refusal by the court to appoint a receiver and a failure to show insolvency of the firm. The defendants showed up the sum of $63,000 assets over all liabilities. The firm will be ready to discharge all claims as they fall due.

W. H. Collins of Butler, who was robbed on Tuesday night, was forced to make an assignment Thursday to Capt. T. H. Frierson. His liabilities are about $3,000, while his assets are said to be about $1,200 or $1,300. There are no preferred creditors. His father, Enoch Collins, is one of the largest creditors, together with Nussbaum & Co., Small & Mallory, Mrs. Johnson, L. Cohen & Co., and others are interested.

Capt. R. Hobbs of Albany has determined to enter upon an experiment which may result beneficially to that section and the entire south. He says that he can't see why jute won't grow in the rich lands of West Dougherty, and he has ordered one pound of the jute seed with which he proposes to make a fair test of the adaptability of the soil and climate to its growth. He will plant it in a rich alluvial soil on his West Dougherty plantation, and devote every necessary attention to its cultivation.

M. M. Willcox, who moved from Telfair county, Georgia, to Texas in 1870, was killed at Bryan, in that state, on Dec. 3. Mr. Willcox was marshal of the town of Bryan, and was attempting to make the arrest of a young man by the name of Earl Knox, who was charged with the crime of burglary. Knox refused to consider himself under arrest, and fired at Marshal Willcox, the latter dying in one hour from the time he was wounded. Knox escaped at the time of the killing, but was captured next day.

At Macon, Thursday, while Tom Woolfolk, the notorious murderer, was walking out in the corridor of the jail, Will Smith, a well-known thief, went into Woolfolk's cell and stole a handkerchief and $3.35 that was tied up in one corner. Woolfolk soon detected the theft and reported it to Jailer Birdsong. Smith tried to throw the money out of the jail, but was detected in the act. Woolfolk always seems to have a little money, which is furnished him by relatives. They claim not to believe in his guilt, and say they will stand by him to the last. Woolfolk is very confident of having a new trial granted him by the supreme court.

A Boy Hero-An Artist-Colored Legislators-Excellent Advice-Cleveland's First Race Journal-Secures $1,000 Attucks-All the News Gathered for "The Gazette's" Readers.
Merry, merry Christmas to you reader.

Wilberforce University students have organized a brass band.

The last issue of the Indianapolis Freeman was a splendid one and Editor Cooper deserves praise.

John Atkinson and Wm. Morrow, two white men in Philadelphia, were attacked and slashed with razors for insulting a young colored girl.

Six colored men were elected to the Texas Legislature November 6. The "Lone Star" State is doing a noble work in the race recognition.

The Edwin Fitler club of Philadelphia has for its president an Afro-American and is composed of the leading Republicans of the city irrespective of color.

At Hopkinsville, Ky., last Sunday, 122 colored converts to the Baptist faith, were baptized in a mill pond. Time, one hour and ten minutes. Rev. John Williams officiated.

The first colored man ever elected to a seat in the Kansas Legislature is Rev. Alfred Fairfax, who was the Republican nominee for Representative in Chatauqua County at the recent election.

The next Ohio Assembly will contain two colored Legislators, Hons. Jere A. Brown, of this city, and W. H. Copeland, of Cincinnati. They were in the last Assembly. Illinois has one, Hon. George Ecton, of Chicago.

There are probably not quite so many newspapers as there were in this country six months ago. The campaign "Yes, we are here and we are here to stay" papers have declined in number. —Recorder.

The colored women of New York city have organized a Woman's Charity and Industrial Club for the help of their colored sisters, and have leased a four-story house as a home for friendless colored girls.

The "American Home Baptist Missionary Society" has lifted the entire debt amounting to $7,800 off the State University at Louisville, Ky., and now Prof. Simmons and his students propose to have a $2,000 jubilee.

At the funeral of Benjamin Fulton, a colored letter carrier of Omaha, Neb., who died Nov. 23, all the pall bearers save one were white, and the letter carriers association escorted the remains from the residence to the church.

A NEGRO'S CRIME.
A NEGROS CRIME.
He Brutally Ravishes a Woman at Wichita, Kansas.
KANSAS CITY. May 22. [Special Telegram]
KANSAS CITY, May 22.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A Wichita, Kan., special says: About 2 o'clock this morning a negro entered the house of a widow named Sophia Stanley, in the north part of the city, and committed a criminal assault upon her. A five-year-old child was the only other occupant of the house. Mrs. Stanley was awakened by a noise at the window, only in time to see the negro jump through the gauze screen. Before she could cry for assistance he had seized her by the throat. She is a slight woman and was unable to offer much resistance. The negro's fingers gradually closed on her throat till she was unconscious. When she regained consciousness the negro had vanished. The neighborhood was alarmed and the police notified, but every effort so far has failed to find her assailant. Three negroes have been taken before her but she could not identify any of them as the man. The excitement is intense and is accompanied with the usual talk of lynching.

PREPARATIONS FOR A MOB.
Last night about 10 o'clock the report was spread upon the street that a mob was about to storm the jail and take out and hang Tom Collins, the man accused of raping Mrs. Standley. Sheriff Hays, fearing that there was more truth than fiction in the report, immediately asked for assistance in guarding the jail, and as many men as he thought necessary were soon furnished and armed. He announced that it was his intention to protect his prisoners, and if a mob called upon him they might expect a very warm reception.

Crowds of people attracted by the expected trouble gathered all around the jail and remained watching for sometime. Quite a party of colored men had, too, gathered in the vicinity, they announced it their purpose to prevent any harm being done to the colored prisoner. The militia, Co. A., K. N. G., were, too, in readiness upon the ground. Scouts were sent out all over the town in order to gain intelligence of the lynchers, but they had at a late hour returned without any satisfactory information as to their numbers or whereabouts.

There was, in fact, a very general preparation for any mob that might have chosen to have called. This fact, no doubt, had a tendency to disconcert any riotous movement that might have been on foot; and so the greater part of the night passed without the expected mob materializing.

STATE VS. TOM COLLINS.
The Collins case came up yesterday in the district court. It is a somewhat noted case and attracted considerable of a crowd in the court room. Among the spectators were to be found very many colored persons, friends of the defendant, all of whom persist in believing him innocent and are there apparently to see that justice is done him.

Tom Collins, the defendant, is accused of committing a rape upon Mrs. Dena Standley the night of May 21st, at her home on North Mosley. The history of the affair is somewhat peculiar and the defendant is held mostly upon circumstantial evidence. On the morning of the 22d Mrs. Standley came to the sheriff's office and showing where she had been scratched and bruised said that a colored man had the night before crawled in through a window of her house and after choking her into insensibility committed the crime in question. An old man of seventy was first arrested, but afterwards discharged. The second arrest was made by officer Webking and the prisoner, Collins. When taken before Mrs. Standley she said that in Collins she recognized her ravisher. He had his preliminary hearing, was bound over to the district court, and has spent the time since then in the county jail. Messrs. Martin and Eckstein and Mr. McMeachan appeared for the defense, County Attorney Jones and Mr. J. W. Adams for the state.

The witnesses for the state were Mrs. Standley, prosecutrix, Officers Webking and Hartzeli, who worked up the case, Albert Thompson, S. W. Bickell and C. A. Clark, all of whom had conversation with the accused on the day following the alleged commission of the crime, Mr. Clark having been instrumental in causing the arrest of Collins.

After the examination of Kansas Jackson; Minnie Maxwell and a man named McDonald, for the defense, the case was continued until this morning at 9 o'clock.

Wichita Beacon: The case of the state of Kansas vs. Tom Collins, accused of raping Mrs. Lena Standley, was set for trial in the district court to-day. Collins is a negro and is accused of breaking into Mrs. Standley's house one night last May and ravishing her. The excitement in the neighborhood of the crime was at a fever heat for several days following Collins' arrest, and threats of lynching were freely indulged in. Several attempts were made to get him out of jail and Sheriff Hayes had to call out the state militia to protect the prisoner. The state officers issued subpoenas for all the witnesses in the case except Mrs. Standley, supposing she would be at the trial when it was called. It now turns out that Mrs. Standley is not in the city, and her whereabouts is not known, unless she is yet in Hutchinson, where she went some time ago. A subpoena will be issued for her.

Leavenworth Times: Jennie Fullerton, daughter of John Fullerton, who resides near Soldier City, created a sensation Saturday by attempting to elope in a rather novel way. Jennie is sixteen years of age, and seems to be yearning for the company of a certain young man. She politely asked him Sunday if he would run away with her. The young man said it would be delightful to do so, or words to that effect. So Saturday Mrs Jennie began to make preparations for
orwords to that effect. So Saturday Miss Jennie began to make preparations for the flight. She didn't pack her Saratoga as most girls do who elope, and jump out of the second story window or slide down a rope into the arms of her lover. That was not her modus operandi. Jennie had an eye for business. This is how she went about it: She first disjointed a bedstead and loaded it into her father's wagon. The necessary bedtick and clothing were then bundled up. Next came plates, knives and forks, cups and saucers for two, a pot, teakettle a can of coal oil, a half bushel of potatoes and many other articles necessary to start to housekeeping. They were all carefully packed in the wagon and then, tired in her best Sunday dress, she hitched up her father's team, which was a spirited one, and started to run away. It was about 8 o'clock in the morning when she left the paternal roof. As she began to raise the dust between her home and the expected lover, she looked like a whole family "bound for Kansas or bust." The lover's heart failed him at the last moment, and he did not meet her "south of town," as ageed. Jennie, nevertheless, pluckily drove on, and it was not until late in the afternoon that her father captured her. The caravan returned to the city just at dusk, and Jennie vows she will select a lover with more nerve next time.
